A: Bit-interleaved coded modulation (BICM) is widely used in multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) wireless systems. However, separating MIMO data detection from channel decoding and only exchanging per-bit soft information discards correlation information among the bits within each transmit vector. We show that the resulting information loss limits the performance of practical one-shot receivers. Even though iterative detection and decoding (IDD) can recover most of this loss, IDD significantly increases receiver complexity and latency. In order to reduce this loss, we propose COrrelation-Informed Logits (COIL), a soft-output format that combines per-bit soft information with pairwise coupling logits for correlated bits. We show how to incorporate these coupling logits into a conventional belief-propagation-based channel decoder, which enables correlation-aware decoding in a one-shot receiver without IDD. We evaluate COIL in a MIMO-BICM system with a conventional low-density parity-check code. For a 4x4 MIMO orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) system, a one-shot linear minimum mean-square error (LMMSE) receiver with COIL outperforms a conventional one-shot unbiased LMMSE receiver by 1.3dB and operates within 0.8dB of four-iteration IDD, while requiring only a single pass through the data detector.

A: Wireless digital twins enable network policies to be evaluated before deployment, but reproducing channel effects within a running protocol stack requires continuous waveform processing under strict timing constraints. We present MIRAGE, a GPU-accelerated channel emulator that applies propagation effects directly to in-phase and quadrature samples exchanged by software 5G New Radio stacks. MIRAGE combines batched multiuser, multiantenna filtering with timestamped shared-memory transport and radio-driver integrations for OpenAirInterface and OCUDU. External propagation models supply channel responses asynchronously, while versioned buffers ensure consistent coefficients within each processing interval. Experiments on one NVIDIA H100 GPU evaluate waveform accuracy, processing time, channel updates, and full-stack traffic delivery. At 61.44 million samples per second, eight single-antenna links, four two-by-two links, and one four-by-four link meet the tested 0.5 ms bidirectional processing criterion. Waveform errors remain within one integer quantization step per component, with no mixed coefficient versions across 16.7 million analyzed slots. Integration with the X5G testbed enables slice resource allocations to be evaluated before deployment. Both evaluated slices ultimately satisfy their throughput caps, requiring one physical reconfiguration under line-of-sight conditions and four under non-line-of-sight conditions. These results demonstrate full-stack policy evaluation and expose prediction errors affecting transfer to a physical network.

A: Direct-to-device (D2D) satellite systems, particularly those based on 3GPP-compliant non-terrestrial networks (NTN), deliver connectivity to standard mobile phones and IoT devices using terrestrial International Mobile Telecommunications (IMT) spectrum. This raises the risk of harmful cross-border interference into incumbent terrestrial IMT networks, an issue considered under Agenda Item 1.13 of the ITU World Radiocommunication Conference 2027 (WRC-27). This paper presents an ITU-R-compliant assessment of aggregate downlink interference from two hypothetical D2D systems operating in Jordan and Iraq into terrestrial IMT user equipment (UE) in Saudi Arabia, operating in the 698-960 MHz band. Unlike prior studies that evaluate a few test points near a simplified ideal tri-border intersection, we distribute multiple victim UEs along realistic national borders within various strips at a distance of 0-40 km from the borders. We compare two satellite selection strategies: highest-elevation and random strategies. The CDF of the interference-to-noise ratio (I/N) together with the intra-system and inter-system aggregation factors are analyzed. Results show that the protection criterion is exceeded up to 88% of the time, requiring up to 27 dB of additional isolation, so coexistence is infeasible without interference mitigation. In general, random selection produces higher interference because low-elevation beams place victims closer to boresight. Two mitigation techniques are then evaluated. A border isolation zone of one cell diameter yields only a moderate improvement under both strategies, whereas a narrow-beam, deep-null phased-array pattern lowers the exceedance to about 40% irrespective of strategy, providing an important input for spectrum regulatory considerations.

However, the implementation of a narrow-beam, deep-null phased-array pattern demonstrated a reduction in the interference rate to around 40%, irrespective of the selection strategy employed. These findings underscore the necessity for effective interference management in D2D satellite systems to achieve coexistence with terrestrial IMT networks.

A_prime: This study examines the impact of Direct-to-Device (D2D) satellite communications within the context of Non-Terrestrial Networks (NTN) as defined by the 3GPP standards. Specifically, the research focuses on the interference caused by D2D operations within the International Mobile Telecommunications (IMT) frequency band, particularly in the 698-960 MHz range, on conventional IMT User Equipment (UE) in Saudi Arabia. To achieve a comprehensive understanding of the interference patterns, a deployment was conducted across the borders of Jordan and Iraq, with victim UEs positioned up to 40 kilometers away from the D2D communication sites. Two methods were employed to select satellites: one using the highest elevation angles and another employing a random selection approach. The analysis of the Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) of the Interference-to-Nominal Signal (I/N) ratio revealed significant interference levels, with protection levels being compromised up to 88% of the time. This necessitates an increase in isolation requirements by up to 27 decibels. The findings indicate that the random selection of satellites exacerbates the interference problem, with low-elevation satellite beams coming perilously close to the operating frequencies of IMT networks. Consequently, the study highlights the critical need for implementing effective mitigation strategies to prevent interference between D2D systems and existing IMT networks, thereby ensuring seamless operation of both technologies.

A: Reflected paths can support localization when line-of-sight (LoS) links are blocked, but their usefulness depends on how accurately the stored model predicts their directions. This paper develops electromagnetic-twin (ET) direction-of-arrival (DoA) localization with a persistent, physically calibrated path-angle field. A nominal floor plan supplies virtual-path geometry, and sparse reference probes at known positions learn a compact directional correction. Field order and regularization are selected from calibration data alone. For each user, unordered DoAs are processed by joint position estimation and one-to-one path association, using assignment-aware multistart search and robust Gauss--Newton refinement. New trusted probes update the stored correction through recursive least squares (RLS), without reprocessing all previous measurements. The analysis establishes calibration rank conditions, objective descent, and conditional information gains from reflected paths, while also distinguishing the decay of initialization bias from the convergence of localization error. Synthetic experiments use 500 queries per operating point. At 50% LoS blockage and $1.5^\circ$ DoA error, the calibrated ET achieves 0.39 m root-mean-square error, versus 0.55 m for nominal geometry. After a wall change, its final error is 0.43 m, versus 0.63 m for a frozen calibrated map. Equal-evidence comparisons show competitive calibrated alternatives and faster abrupt-change recovery with sliding-window updates than with the configured RLS. The results support reusable directional calibration, not a universally superior map or update rule, and validation is limited to synthetic first-order reflections with trusted calibration labels.

A: The upper mid-band, also known as Frequency Range 3 (FR3), spans 7.125-24.25 GHz and is a key candidate band for sixth-generation (6G) wireless communications. However, channel measurements in industrial environments remain scarce, and the 3GPP indoor-factory (InF) channel model, developed for omnidirectional antennas, has yet to be validated across the FR3 band. This paper presents a wideband channel measurement campaign in an industrial production hall, covering 135 line-of-sight (LOS) positions at 1-18 m and 30 non-line-of-sight (NLOS) positions behind an industrial robot at 2.5-16.5 m across 6-12 GHz. In LOS, the path-loss exponent ranged from 1.87 to 2.12, and the close-in fits agreed with the 3GPP InF-LOS model to within approximately 2 dB. However, shadow fading was only 1.4-1.7 dB, compared with the model's 4.3 dB. In NLOS, the robot caused an excess loss that increased from 10.3 to 13.0 dB between 6.5 and 11.5 GHz, consistent with diffraction. Blocking the direct path raised the mean directional delay spread from approximately 5 to 25 ns, close to omnidirectional values. These results indicate that the 3GPP InF model captures mean LOS path loss well but overestimates the variability of beam-aligned FR3 links, and that blockage loss in FR3 is frequency dependent. The dataset and processing code are publicly available.

A: Wireless foundation models learn reusable representations across tasks, configurations, and deployment environments. Their pretraining requires environmental breadth, yet wireless datasets often sample few sites densely. We introduce Channels4World, a scene-centered dataset of 100,000 distinct outdoor RF scenes and a procedural method for generating them. Each scene links a generated environment and RF material assignments to 32 base-station (BS) positions, 16,384 UE positions, and aligned variable-length multipath and ordered interaction records at 3.5 and 7~GHz. The corpus comprises 52.43 billion physical BS-UE pairs, 104.86 billion frequency-specific evaluations, and a 29.14-TB packaged payload. Scene identity aligns geometry, placements, channels, and interactions across frequencies, allowing environmental breadth and within-scene observation density to vary independently. The public release offers predefined subsets at multiple scales and separate access to corpus components. A deterministic 90K/10K scene-level train-test split keeps both frequencies and all scene components together. We characterize morphology, RF materials, and transceiver placement across three generation profiles. Controlled propagation and path-retention analyses show that diffraction materially affects retained-link availability and multipath structure, while the retention policy reduces storage substantially with little loss in represented aggregate power. Under matched training exposure, models trained on broader scene collections perform better on held-out scenes, although an equal-episode control shows that scene count alone cannot explain the gain. By making environmental breadth explicit and controllable, Channels4World supports the development and evaluation of wireless foundation models for generalization across deployment environments.

A: Future wireless systems for indoor applications are expected to extend their operating frequencies from sub-6 GHz to mid-band and millimeter wave (mmWave) frequencies to support higher data rates. To characterize the frequency-dependent propagation behavior across these bands, multi-band channel measurements are essential. In this work, we conduct double-directional multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) channel measurements in an indoor environment to enable a consistent comparison across three frequency bands. A: Low Earth orbit (LEO) satellite signals have recently attracted increasing attention as opportunistic signals for positioning, navigation, and timing. In contrast, passive software-defined radio (SDR) monitoring systems often retain only time-frequency power scans, in which LEO Doppler traces appear as unlabeled ridges without raw IQ samples or identifiable signal structures. This paper proposes a clock-shift-aided segment-based blind Doppler matching method that associates unlabeled Doppler traces with candidate satellites predicted using two-line element (TLE) data. The proposed framework consists of slope-consistent Doppler segment generation, clock-shift-aided temporal alignment, and multi-metric satellite matching based on Doppler-rate and trajectory-shape consistency. The proposed method was evaluated using a three-hour subset of open Starlink/OneWeb monitoring data collected in the United Kingdom. The clock-offset search selected an effective offset of +19 s, for which 56 of 69 segments had at least one slope-compatible candidate, compared with 19 segments at zero shift. Using the resulting satellite associations, the batch positioning error over the full three-hour period was 104.2 m, whereas the RMSE-based and slope-based simple-segment baselines failed to converge near the reference receiver location.

A: Semantic error control coding (SECC) can correct the residual errors of a standard channel code with a foundation model that supplies a prior on the source content, but existing SECC schemes are designed for text. In this paper, we develop SECC for image transmission with spatial token interleaving and a two-pass belief propagation (BP) schedule. At the transmitter, a vector-quantized (VQ) tokenizer converts an image into tokens, which are transmitted in multiple low-density parity-check (LDPC) code blocks of fifth-generation New Radio (5G NR). In raster order, a block that BP fails to decode corrupts consecutive token rows, so the interleaver reorders the tokens such that adjacent tokens are carried by different blocks, without additional transmitted bits. At the receiver, after the first BP pass, token recovery fuses the token probabilities given by BP with the predictions of the autoregressive model Emu3-Gen, and the second BP pass decodes each block again with the fused distributions as priors on the information bits. On Kodak24 at 0.5 channel uses per pixel and a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of 0.15 dB, the second pass removes 92% of the token errors left by token recovery, and interleaving reduces the final token error rate by 88%. At medium to high SNR, the proposed receiver exceeds deep joint source--channel coding baselines with the same channel uses by at least 1.2 dB in peak signal-to-noise ratio.

A: We design and evaluate a site-specific neural receiver for the 5G New Radio (NR) uplink. A corridor digital twin built from a radar scan and refined manually provides 28,671 ray-traced channel records for training an eight-round convolutional graph neural network with pilot-aware inputs and auxiliary channel supervision. The GPU on NVIDIA DGX Spark evaluates time--frequency convolutions in parallel across the received grid to accelerate inference. The receiver uses the standard NR uplink waveform and reference signals and feeds soft bits to the existing transport-block decoder. In over-the-air tests with NI USRP B210 radios under common radio settings, the site-trained receiver achieves the highest mean uplink rate at all five positions. At a non-line-of-sight corner, it reaches 16.2 Mb/s, compared with 4.1 Mb/s for the conventional receiver and 2.4 Mb/s for the 3GPP-trained neural receiver. These results demonstrate the feasibility of integrating neural reception into the 5G NR physical layer and show its potential for AI-RAN deployments.

A: Music source separation extracts vocals and instruments from a mixed recording, enabling remixing, content production, and music analysis. Existing systems commonly operate on waveforms or full-band spectrograms. Waveform inputs contain many samples even in short segments, whereas a single spectrogram resolution imposes a shared time-frequency resolution trade-off across frequency ranges. We propose SubRoFormer, a Transformer-based system comprising a subband module and a residual RoFormer module. The subband module decomposes the mixture into frequency-localized, lower-rate signals for separation. It then reconstructs the target waveforms from the estimated subbands. The residual RoFormer module models temporal and cross-band relationships on temporally compressed features. It combines this context with fine-rate features through gated residual fusion to estimate source-specific complex masks. On the MUSDB18-HQ test set, training only on MUSDB18-HQ yields an average signal-to-distortion ratio (SDR) of 10.63 dB across four stems using target-specific models, achieving state-of-the-art performance among the compared systems without extra training data. With 500 additional training songs, a single model jointly separating all four stems achieves an average SDR of 11.59 dB, establishing state-of-the-art performance among the compared single-model multi-stem systems trained with extra data. Code and checkpoints are released at https://github.com/ArchiMickey/SubRoformer.

The second part, residual RoFormer, looks at the timing and relationships between different frequencies. This helps to predict complex masks for each sound source. Our tests on the MUSDB18-HQ dataset show that when we only use MUSDB18-HQ for training, we get an average SDR of 10.63 dB for separating four different sound parts. A: Repeatable test setups support the development and evaluation of integrated sensing and communications (ISAC) hardware and algorithms. Commercial radar target simulators are expensive, while sub-6 GHz ISAC experiments often need only tens of megahertz of bandwidth within their available spectrum allocation. This makes simpler, low-cost test hardware attractive. We present a low-cost, open-source radar target simulator based on an ADALM-Pluto without hardware modification, supporting four independently configurable targets and analog bandwidths up to 56 MHz. The FPGA generates echoes with independent delays, Doppler shifts and gains, using fractional-delay filters for sub-sample adjustment. For motion-consistent echoes, delay and carrier phase are updated together to reproduce both changing range and frequency-dependent Doppler shifts. Over-the-air measurements demonstrate simultaneous echoes, sub-sample delay adjustment, and smooth target motion between sample positions. The FPGA source, firmware and on-device web interface are publicly available.

A: We study the least-cost co-expansion of power distribution networks and public charging ports to accommodate the growth of electric vehicles (EVs). Our approach, MAC+, exploits the flexibility of charging along each EV's itinerary and coordinates it across the fleet to reduce the peak violations of each feeder's hosting capacity and port capacity. This coordination is an extremely large, spatio-temporally coupled optimization problem with binary plug-in variables. We solve it by iterated price response (IPR), which repeatedly posts a two-tier tariff on feeder load and port occupancy, lets millions of EVs best-respond in parallel, and certifies the optimality gap at every iteration. We develop a custom exact dynamic-programming algorithm that solves each EV's best-response problem, a mixed-integer quadratic program, about 20 times faster than off-the-shelf solvers. The case study covers the San Francisco Bay Area at 30% EV adoption, with 1.8 million EVs on week-long itineraries and 1,303 feeder service regions, each with a utility-published hosting capacity and a port capacity set by its existing public ports. On this instance, IPR reaches a certified gap below 10% in a few hours. MAC+ saves about $15 billion of the upgrade investment that unmanaged charging would require. It also needs over 90% less investment than charging that is fully coordinated but flexible only within each session, and over 80% less than charging that is flexible along the itinerary but uncoordinated.

With IPR, we set a two-tier tariff for feeder load and port occupancy, enabling the collective best-response of millions of EVs while ensuring each iteration's optimization gap is certified. We introduce a novel dynamic-programming algorithm tailored for this purpose, which effectively handles each EV's best-response scenario, a mixed-integer quadratic problem, at speeds roughly 20 times faster than conventional solvers. A: Heterogeneous air-ground teams can use aerial sensing to address the limited range and viewpoint of ground-vehicle sensors, but deciding when the UGV needs assistance and what information the UAV should collect remains a challenge. This paper presents a planner-conditioned air-ground assistance method that evaluates how uncertain map information affects the UGV's current MPPI rollouts. When navigation remains degraded, we score the same rollouts under resolved map hypotheses, select the map layer with the largest useful improvement, request the corresponding aerial measurement, fuse the returned information, and replan. Unlike approaches driven by fixed support roles, task structure, or uncertainty alone, our method conditions assistance on whether resolving uncertainty improves predicted ground navigation. Across 180 simulation trials on three off-road routes, the method achieves 98.9% goal attainment while reducing mean UAV flight time by 87.7% relative to continuous greedy aerial mapping. Aggregated across the routes, each second of estimated UAV flight time saves 2.94 s of UGV navigation time. Field experiments spanning approximately 2 km of UGV operation demonstrate uncertainty resolution and successful navigation recovery.

If the UGVs' navigation is still degraded, we score various rollouts against hypothetically resolved maps, choose the map layer that brings the most substantial benefit, then ask for that aerial measurement from the UAV. We merge the new info with existing data and redo the plan. Our unique approach isn't just reliant on the role of UAVs, task design, or uncertainty; we base help on whether fixing uncertainty could improve the UGV's next navigation move. In the real world, with about 2 km of UGV trail, our work helps clarify uncertainties and rescues navigation problems. Each second saved on the estimated UAV flight time means a 2.94 second boost in UGV travel time.

A: This paper presents a novel method for converting the divergent Gaussian intensity distribution of a millimeter-wave source into a uniform (flat-top) distribution using a single curved surface. The proposed method combines the surface profile of a collimator with that of a beam shaper. To validate the method, the profile of a single-sided (plano-convex) lens is derived and placed 52 mm in front of a conical horn antenna operating at 100 GHz. The lens transforms the Gaussian radiation of the horn, with an incident beam radius of 11.9 mm, into a uniform beam with a radius of 400 mm at a distance of 3 m. The lens surface profile is optimized using a full-wave-simulation-based procedure, and the resulting output beam is compared with that of a previously designed double-sided (concave-convex) lens. Simulation results show that, within the desired field of view, the optimized single-sided lens produces a flat-top intensity distribution with satisfactory ripple and roll-off. Finally, the sensitivity of the optimized lens to frequency variation is investigated. The proposed lens is suitable for generating uniform illumination in active stand-off millimeter-wave imaging systems.

A: The increasing penetration of converter-interfaced generation reduces system inertia, short-circuit strength, and voltage support. European grid codes, including the ENTSO-E Network Code on Requirements for Generators and the ACER Demand Connection Code, now define disturbance-based validation procedures for grid-forming (GFM) generation and converter-based demand. Commercial RMS tools, however, lack an integrated workflow aligned with these recent requirements. This paper presents an automated Python-PowerFactory compliance toolbox and an RMS test bench for a co-located system comprising a 1 MW GFM photovoltaic (PV) plant, a 0.3 MW GFM battery energy storage system (BESS), and a 1 MW converter-interfaced dynamic load at a 20 kV point of common coupling fed from a 110 kV grid. Extended virtual synchronous machine models and a DCC-oriented load model are tested in batch, with results automatically extracted and plotted for assessment. Results show compliant RMS performance for the slower, electromechanical tests, while the paper identifies which tests require complementary electromagnetic transient (EMT) verification.

A: In this paper, a novel, to our knowledge, analytical approach is introduced for the design of a single-sided plano-convex lens (PCL) capable of terahertz (THz) flat-top beam shaping in the Fresnel region. The lens profile, derived from geometrical optics principles, integrates collimating and beam-shaping functions into a single optical surface, thereby simplifying fabrication. The efficiency of the method is demonstrated by designing two PCLs that convert a divergent Gaussian beam from a monochromatic THz source (at 100 and 200 GHz) into flat-top beams with target radii of 400 and 500 mm at distances of 3 and 4 m, respectively. The resulting fields, evaluated through analytical, integral equation, and finite element techniques, are shown to be comparable to those produced by a conventional double-sided concave-convex lens. Furthermore, the sensitivity of the design to frequency and alignment variations is investigated, confirming the robustness of this single-curvature approach for integration into practical THz imaging systems.

A: Patient-specific airway modelling requires geometrically consistent lumen surfaces with identifiable boundaries and support for controlled anatomical modifications. We present CT-RespGeomLib, a deterministic framework that converts CT airway masks into two complementary representations: an editable assembly of semantically labelled pipe and junction blocks connected through canonical shared ports, and a fused lumen surface reconstructed from tapered implicit primitives with validated port-to-boundary loop correspondence. The parametric representation further enables localised modelling of airway stenosis and dilation without re-segmentation. Evaluated on 42 reference airway masks from ATM22 (15 cases) and AeroPath (27 cases), the framework produced 37 topologically accepted reconstructions, with a median port-to-loop distance of 0.123 mm across 2174 matched ports. Reconstructed and reference equivalent radii showed strong agreement ($R^2 = 0.976$), with a mean bias of -0.414 mm arising primarily from the circular, inscribed-radius representation. Controlled pathology modelling generated 40 variants across five patient-specific geometries, including 25-75% stenosis and 50% dilation at tracheal and main-bronchus locations. Prescribed radius changes were reproduced with a mean absolute ratio error of 0.0056, while the median 95th-percentile deviation outside the modified region was 0.111 mm. Downstream applicability was demonstrated through volume meshing and an OpenFOAM simulation with individually prescribed model-based resistance conditions at 62 outlets. Although additional surface preparation may be required for numerical meshing, CT-RespGeomLib provides a reproducible framework for CT-derived airway reconstruction, quantitative boundary validation and controlled geometric pathology modelling.

The match-up between our reconstructed surfaces and the real ones showed a strong fit ($R^2 = 0.976$), though there's a slight average bias of -0.414 mm mainly due to the inner circular shape. We made changes to simulate pathologies like 25-75% airway narrowing or 50% expansion in the trachea and main bronchus for five individuals, and our results hold up with a mean error of 0.0056 and a median 95th-percentile variation of 0.111 mm. A: Oscillatory power components in AI data-center demand can produce large frequency deviations when they coincide with vulnerable grid modes. Mode-aware hybrid energy storage systems (HESSs) can selectively suppress these components, but their effectiveness degrades when the grid mode changes while the control target remains fixed. This paper proposes a closed-loop grid-mode-adaptive HESS control framework that integrates measurement-based modal identification with mode-selective control. A sliding-window N4SID estimator identifies the local grid dynamics from grid-side power and frequency measurements, and the resulting natural-frequency estimate is used to retune the modal suppression branch assigned to the supercapacitor. The framework is evaluated under a grid-mode shift from 0.50 to 1.35Hz while maintaining equal physical damping and approximately equal load excitation at both frequencies. Compared with the fixed-target controller, the adaptive method reduces the post-change grid-side modal power component from 8.78 to 2.02MW, corresponding to a 76.94% reduction, and substantially lowers the resulting frequency deviation.

So, we're working on a closed-loop control setup that adapts to the grid's changing modes, using measurements to figure out the grid's behavior and tweaking the control for the supercapacitor accordingly. We tested this approach as the grid's weak spot moved from 0.50 to 1.35Hz, with the same level of damping and roughly the same load. Perception extracts wall lines from each scan with RANSAC and total least squares, with per-line uncertainty. The same line front end feeds two estimators: an Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) that localizes against a line map built from the maze mesh, and an EKF SLAM variant that builds the line map online. Planning runs online on an inflated occupancy grid with A* plus line-of-sight shortcutting, or with a forward-only Hybrid A*. In simulation, the robot drives a 135 m route through the maze with 1.0 cm localization RMSE against the known map and 24 cm in SLAM mode, the planner returns a path in 6 ms, and the NMPC solves in 11.7 ms on average, never exceeding its 80 ms budget.

A: Many rehabilitation robots execute prescribed motions using reactive tracking controllers that do not explicitly incorporate the user's instantaneous human-ground interaction. This paper presents Ground Reaction Force-Aware Model Predictive Control (GRF-MPC), a framework for upright physical assistance. By integrating live GRF and center of pressure (CoP) measurements directly into a human centroidal dynamics model, GRF-MPC formulates a real-time quadratic program (QP) that optimizes assistive forces and moments over a receding horizon. We deployed GRF-MPC on the Robotic Upright Stand Trainer (RobUST) in an underactuated 4-cable configuration and evaluated it against a fully actuated 8-cable Cartesian impedance baseline in nearly 300 trials across six healthy participants. Across tasks spanning impulsive perturbations, lunge trajectories, and voluntary limits of stability, GRF-MPC reduced peak planar center-of-mass (CoM) error by 19.6% during perturbations, lowered trajectory tracking error by 24.1%, required 28.7% less net mechanical work, and permitted a 45.9% greater normalized voluntary excursion area. The underlying QP solves in under 1 ms, comfortably enabling 100 Hz replanning and demonstrating that incorporating live human-ground interaction into predictive control yields stronger, more transparent physical assistance with half the actuators.

Utilizing real-time data from ground reaction forces (GRF) and center of pressure (CoP), GRF-MPC calculates optimal forces and moments through a quadratic program (QP) formulation. We developed the Ground Reaction Force-Minimal Polynomial Control (GRF-MPC) method, which utilizes real-time Ground Reaction Forces (GRFs) and Center of Pressure (CoP) data to optimize the interaction between the human subject and the robotic system. A: Autonomous racing provides a demanding testbed for collision avoidance under tight geometric and computational constraints. Building on a recent conference contribution and a master's dissertation, LACART combines lookahead-based control barrier functions (CBFs), a relaxed control Lyapunov function (CLF), and quadratic programming (QP) to modify nominal vehicle commands for obstacle avoidance and reference tracking. The method handles circular obstacles and track boundaries in a common optimisation layer. Comparative simulation results against Huang \emph{et al.} \cite{r9} show similar full-track paths and lower median computation times: 0.31 versus 0.33 ms per step and 0.023 versus 0.025 ms per QP solve. The dissertation further demonstrates a 1:43-scale vehicle with camera-based estimation and wireless actuation at a reported 25 Hz control rate. We identify the conditions linking lookahead-point clearance to body clearance, illustrate hardware limitations, and propose a recorded demonstration of safety intervention and recovery. The contribution targets ground-robot collision avoidance and real-time safety monitoring.

We're digging into what it takes to keep the lookahead clearance and body clearance in sync, figuring out the gear limitations, and even recorded how we handle safety checks and bounce back from mishaps. A: Monitoring the relative radiometric stability of the European Space Agency's BIOMASS P-band synthetic aperture radar (SAR) requires separating instrumental and processing effects from temporal changes in the scene backscatter. This study investigates the use of permanent scatterers (PSs) as opportunistic references for estimating residual radiometric gains without dedicated calibration targets. The PS-based calibration (PSCal) framework combines amplitude-based scatterer selection with iterative maximum-likelihood gain estimation. Simulations assess detection and estimation performance under the limited number of acquisitions available in BIOMASS stacks, highlighting the importance of stringent selection thresholds and the dependence of estimation accuracy on scatterer abundance and signal-to-noise ratio. The approach is applied to datasets over Nairobi, Kenya, and Cordoba, Argentina. Over Nairobi, PSCal identifies an approximately 1 dB radiometric anomaly subsequently traced to a defect in radio-frequency interference mitigation, while the remaining acquisitions exhibit estimated gain variations generally within 0.1 dB. Over Cordoba, twelve acquisitions spanning two mission phases separated by approximately eight months yield residual gain variations on the order of 0.1 dB despite pronounced changes in the scene backscatter and acquisition geometry. Results were observed to be consistent with measurements from the BIOMASS Calibration Transponder (BCT) installed in New Norcia (Australia). These results demonstrate the potential of carefully selected P-band PSs to complement dedicated calibration infrastructure for relative radiometric monitoring and the detection of processing anomalies.

By running simulations with the limited data we got from the BIOMASS stacks, we see how crucial it is to be strict about our PS selection and how the accuracy depends on the number of PSs and how clear they are. The findings matched up with the BIOMASS Calibration Transponder (BCT) data from New Norcia. The research employs Permanent Scatterers (PSs) as reference points to assess and mitigate radiometric variations, thereby avoiding the use of dedicated calibration targets. A novel approach, termed PS-Based Calibration (PSCal), involves selecting PSs based on their amplitude characteristics and iteratively determining the maximum likelihood gain values. Simulations were conducted to evaluate the performance of the PSCal method under conditions of limited data availability, highlighting the importance of stringent selection criteria and the accuracy of gain estimation based on the number of available PSs and signal clarity. Field experiments were carried out in Nairobi and Cordoba, where the PSCal method was applied to BIOMASS data collected over multiple acquisitions. In Nairobi, a significant 1 dB anomaly was observed due to RF interference, whereas in Cordoba, consistent gain adjustments of approximately 0.1 dB were noted despite substantial scene and acquisition variations. These findings align with observations from the BIOMASS Calibration Transponder (BCT) located in New Norcia, Australia, suggesting that the PSCal method effectively enhances the reliability of radiometric measurements and aids in detecting processing anomalies.

A: Pretrained Earth observation models may reduce the effort needed to map surface water, but their value depends on the alternative against which they are compared. We evaluated Prithvi-EO-2.0-Tiny using the 446 hand-labeled Sentinel-2 chips from 11 flood events in Sen1Floods11. A fine-tuned model, a frozen-encoder model, and an identical randomly initialized architecture were compared with a similarly sized U-Net, a larger Prithvi model, and spectral-index thresholds. Experiments varied the number of training chips, excluded events from model fitting, and measured computational cost and prediction reliability. With 252 training chips, U-Net achieved a water intersection-over-union (IoU) of 0.856 on the official test set, compared with 0.833 for fine-tuned Prithvi-Tiny. Pretraining improved the tiny transformer over random initialization by a reported 0.046 IoU with 25 training chips and 0.023 with 252 chips, but did not reverse the U-Net ranking. Across 11 event-exclusion evaluations, mean IoU was 0.768 for fine-tuned Prithvi-Tiny and 0.777 for U-Net; the paired interval included zero. Fine-tuned Prithvi-Tiny processed a 512x512-pixel chip in 16.1 ms on a GPU and 258 ms on a laptop CPU, compared with 30.6 and 665 ms for U-Net. Errors were concentrated near water boundaries, and high predictive entropy identified many, but not all, erroneous pixels. These results support a specific role for compact pretrained models: lower measured computational demand with competitive accuracy, rather than consistent superiority. Event-dependent performance, shared hyperparameter selection, and the distinction between observed water and newly inundated land delimit the conclusions.

This suggests that small pretrained models can be good for lower computational costs and fairly accurate results, rather than always being the best choice. We have to consider event-specific performance, consistent parameter choices, and clear water vs. inundated land distinctions.

Specifically, four models—fine-tuned Prithvi-EO-2.0-Tiny, frozen-encoder Prithvi-EO-2.0-Tiny, untrained Prithvi-Tiny, and U-Net—were evaluated using 446 hand-labeled Sentinel-2 chips from 11 flood events in the Sen1Floods11 dataset. The performance of these models was assessed based on Intersection over Union (IoU) scores on an official test set, considering varying numbers of training chips and excluding some flood events during model fitting. The results indicated that the U-Net achieved a water IoU of 0.856 with 252 training chips, surpassing the fine-tuned Prithvi-EO-2.0-Tiny by 0.023 IoU. Despite pretraining, the untrained Prithvi-Tiny model only improved by 0.046 IoU when using 25 chips, maintaining a significant advantage over the U-Net. When evaluating the models' performance under different conditions, the fine-tuned Prithvi-EO-2.0-Tiny yielded a mean IoU of 0.768, whereas the U-Net produced a mean IoU of 0.777. Conversely, the U-Net required 30.6 milliseconds and 665 milliseconds for the same task, respectively. A: LOL-v1 and LOLv2-Real are the standard benchmarks for supervised low-light image enhancement, and several leading methods ship hand-set test-time adjustments with their evaluation scripts. We audit both benchmarks with 18 public checkpoints of eight methods under one metric implementation that reproduces every published number to within 0.09 dB, and find that their test labels differ from their training labels. (i) The 15 LOL-v1 test labels are rendered differently: the same captures appear in LOLv2 with labels of identical luminance but 1.48x lower saturation, and LOL-v1's own training labels match the LOLv2 rendering; we confirm this on the official release. (ii) The LOLv2-Real test set is the contiguous block of images 690-789, whose labels are 14% darker than the training labels (Cliff's delta = -0.45, p < 1e-12) with no comparable shift in the input statistics we examined; methods trained without any labels score up to 5.5 dB higher on test than on train. (iii) All 15 LOL-v1 test inputs reappear in LOLv2-Real, 12 in its training set. The released test-time settings are consistent with compensating for these shifts. Separating what can be calibrated on training data from what only test-set tuning finds, the test-only residual has median 0.00 dB on LOLv2-Syn, which has no shift, but 0.37 dB on LOL-v1 and 0.92 dB on LOLv2-Real (up to 3.9 dB). Under the shift, test-set checkpoint selection inflates a from-scratch model by 0.9-2.0 dB, and removing the released settings changes which method ranks first. We give concrete reporting recommendations.

Utilizing 18 publicly available datasets from eight distinct methodologies, our analysis reveals that both models have been benchmarked rigorously. The precision of our evaluation metrics is noteworthy, achieving a deviation of less than 0.09 dB. Notably, discrepancies were observed between the 15 test labels from LOL-v1 and those from LOLv2. Specifically, images appearing in LOLv2 exhibit significantly reduced contrast levels, approximately 1.48 times lower, compared to their counterparts in LOL-v1. This phenomenon is corroborated by the official documentation. Additionally, a subset of 690-789 images from LOLv2-Real showed a substantial decrease in brightness, with a Cliff's delta value of -0.45, indicating a statistically significant difference (p < 1e-12). These findings suggest that the models trained without explicit low-light training labels achieved superior performance on the test set, demonstrating a learning curve that surpasses expectations. Furthermore, while almost all 15 LOL-v1 test images were present in the LOLv2-Real dataset, only 12 of them were included in the training set. The test-time settings employed in LOLv2-Syn, characterized by the absence of label changes, resulted in a median performance of 0.00 dB. In contrast, when comparing LOL-v1 and LOLv2-Real, the median performances were 0.37 dB and 0.92 dB, respectively, with the latter reaching a peak of 3.9 dB. These observations highlight the potential impact of data distribution and label availability on model performance in low-light image enhancement tasks.

A: Deep-learning unrolled networks are the leading approach to accelerated MRI reconstruction. State-of-the-art models such as PromptMR+ learn a distinct block for every cascade, so their size grows with the number of cascades. Sharing one block across iterations avoids adding parameters, but earlier shared-weight models typically used a tiny block and produced worse images than models with distinct weights. Therefore, it remained unclear whether weight sharing itself or the choice of block was the problem. Recent advances in looped transformers, which reuse the same block across layers, show that they can match or outperform their distinct-weight counterparts on several tasks. Motivated by this, we propose LoopMR, which reuses a single Restormer block at every iteration as its core. Besides the current image estimate, the block receives data-consistency inputs and latent images. On four datasets covering the brain (CC359), knee (fastMRI), heart (CMRxRecon2023) and carotid (in-house), LoopMR significantly outperforms E2E-VarNet, PromptMR and PromptMR+ in PSNR and SSIM at every acceleration factor (p < 0.01), with about 1/9 of PromptMR+'s parameters (10.3M versus 92.9M). It also keeps its lead at unseen acceleration factors and on an unseen dataset. With our transformer block, the shared model matches or outperforms its distinct-weight counterpart at 6, 12 and 24 iterations. At a fixed number of iterations, shared transformer blocks match or outperform their distinct-weight versions, while shared CNN blocks perform worse. These results suggest that looping one well-chosen block can outperform stacking distinct cascades in MRI reconstruction, with a fraction of the parameters.

Previous research has demonstrated that models such as PromptMR+ employ separate blocks for each step in MRI reconstruction, leading to an increasing number of blocks as additional steps are incorporated. However, there remains uncertainty regarding whether it is the shared weights or the selection of block sizes that contribute to performance limitations. To address these challenges, we introduce LoopMR, which utilizes a single shared block at each layer of the network architecture. Our evaluation of LoopMR was conducted across four diverse datasets: CC359 for brain scans, fastMRI for knee examinations, CMRxRecon2023 for heart scans, and in-house data for carotid imaging. The results indicate that LoopMR significantly outperforms existing models, including E2E-VarNet, PromptMR, and PromptMR+, in terms of peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) and structural similarity index measure (SSIM). Notably, LoopMR achieves superior performance with a substantially reduced parameter count, reducing the model size from 92.9 million parameters to 10.3 million parameters in comparison to PromptMR+. Furthermore, LoopMR demonstrates robust generalization capabilities, maintaining its effectiveness across various datasets and higher acceleration levels. These findings suggest that a single shared block configuration can yield superior performance compared to models employing multiple distinct blocks, thereby highlighting the potential advantages of shared architecture designs in MRI reconstruction tasks.

A_prime: This study explores the application of looped transformers in deep-learning unrolled networks for accelerating medical imaging processing, specifically focusing on Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) applications. Previous research has shown that stacking multiple blocks within models like PromptMR+ can lead to increased computational complexity and reduced performance due to decreased model efficiency. To address these limitations, a novel approach termed LoopMR was developed, incorporating a single Restormer block across all iterations. The efficacy of this method was evaluated across various clinical datasets, including brain (CC359), knee (fastMRI), heart (CMRxRecon2023), and carotid (in-house dataset) scans. Comparative analysis revealed that LoopMR achieved superior performance metrics such as Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) and Structural Similarity Index Measure (SSIM) values, surpassing established methods such as E2E-VarNet and PromptMR+ in terms of statistical significance (p < 0.01). Furthermore, LoopMR demonstrated remarkable scalability, maintaining high performance even when tested with new datasets and varying computational requirements. Notably, the proposed approach required significantly fewer parameters (10.3 million compared to 92.9 million for PromptMR+) while offering comparable or superior results. These findings suggest that the utilization of looped transformers, particularly the Restormer block, can effectively enhance the efficiency and adaptability of deep-learning unrolled networks in medical imaging applications.

A: Image-guided surgery (IGS) depends on accurate tracking of surgical instruments to provide real-time navigation relative to anatomical structures. Commercial stereo infrared trackers are accurate but prone to occlusion and cost-prohibitive for many settings. This work presents LARK, a multi-camera optical tracking system using commodity RGB hardware and multi-view redundancy and fusion. We develop and evaluate two complete tracking methods: multi-view monocular pose fusion and multi-view triangulation. Both methods are assessed under varying occlusion levels using a precision-machined grid and an anatomical head phantom, and compared against a gold-standard stereo infrared system. With five cameras and adaptive Kalman filtering, LARK achieves median target registration errors of 0.64 mm for point localization with triangulation and 0.73 mm for trajectory tracking with pose fusion on the machined grid. Camera-subset experiments show graceful degradation in adaptive pose-fusion accuracy as fewer views remain available. With tracking hardware costing under $1,000 USD, LARK provides a low-cost platform for image-guided surgery research. Hardware designs and software are publicly available at https://nist.mni.mcgill.ca/software/ , and datasets at https://nist.mni.mcgill.ca/data/ .

Methods: Sampling theory was used to derive analytical frame-rate bounds required for kinematic feature fidelity. Results: Sinc interpolation yielded lower median mean absolute error than spline (0.29 vs 0.52 pixels), with 85% of recordings (47/55) versus 45% (25/55) below 0.5 pixels. These challenges stem from the complex interplay between lateral fold movements and longitudinal opening, complicating direct measurement. This research focuses on displacement waveforms, which, despite offering a viable approach, are subject to spatial and temporal inaccuracies. To mitigate these issues, we employed Kalman smoothing and various interpolation techniques, including sinc and spline methods. Experiments were conducted on a set of 4000 fps sample recordings (N=55) and a higher resolution 16000 fps dataset (N=12), comparing noise reduction capabilities across a range of frame rates from 2000 to 8000 fps. The findings revealed that sinc interpolation yielded superior precision compared to spline interpolation, with a median median absolute error difference of 0.23 pixels (0.29 vs. 0.52 pixels). Furthermore, when analyzing kinematic features, Kalman-sinc smoothing demonstrated superior performance to FFT-sinc smoothing, particularly at specific frame rates. Specifically, for velocity and open quotient (OQ) calculations, a frame rate of approximately 8000 fps was recommended. Conversely, for high lateral displacement measurements, a frame rate of 2000 fps proved effective, while a frame rate of 8000 fps was suggested for reliable OQ assessments.

A: Single-image HDR reconstruction requires inferring missing detail while preserving the visible content of an LDR image. Differences in sensor dynamic range and exposure cause LDR images to lose varying amounts of information in shadows and highlights. We present ExpandDiff, a conditional diffusion pipeline that jointly reconstructs clipped shadows and highlights. To account for this variation, we introduce Dynamic Clipping Synthesis (DCS), which randomly samples shadow and highlight clipping percentiles when constructing training inputs from HDR targets. A pixel-space diffusion model guided by spatially-adaptive normalization then predicts perceptually encoded HDR through a bounded output head, reconstructing both clipping directions in one sampling trajectory. On the SI-HDR benchmark, ExpandDiff variants improve HDR reconstruction accuracy by 3.43 dB in PU21-PSNR over the strongest evaluated competing method, and by 7.34 dB under two-sided clipping. The code and supplementary material are available at https://memreandiran.github.io/expanddiff/.

A_prime: This study addresses the challenge of enhancing low-dynamic-range (LDR) images to produce high-dynamic-range (HDR) images through single-image synthesis. The existing limitations of conventional imaging equipment, particularly their restricted dynamic range and exposure capabilities, necessitate the development of advanced techniques to capture and preserve fine details in both shadowy and brightly illuminated regions. To tackle this issue, a novel approach named ExpandDiff has been proposed. ExpandDiff utilizes Conditional Diffusion to restore and amplify the shadow and highlight areas of LDR images. This process involves Dynamic Clipping Synthesis (DCS), which randomly selects percentile values for shadowy and bright regions during the generation of training data from high-fidelity HDR images. The core of ExpandDiff is a pixel-space diffusion model equipped with a spatial normalizer, designed to encode and predict the HDR content in a manner that simultaneously enhances both shadows and highlights. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that the ExpandDiff variants achieve superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods, achieving a peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) improvement of 3.43 dB over the best-performing alternative in the Publicly Available Dataset 21 (PU21) benchmark and an additional 7.34 dB when considering both shadow and highlight clipping. A: Super-resolution networks are trained for one magnification factor, so several output resolutions require several models. We propose PMS-SR, a progressive single-input multiple-output network that produces x2, x4, and x8 results in one forward pass, with a Transformer backbone on the low-resolution grid. In Stage 1, each scale is predicted as a residual over the detached bicubic upsampling of the previous scale's prediction. With Dirac and zero initialization, training starts exactly from the bicubic cascade, and each head adds only the band the previous scale lacks. In Stage 2, inter-scale mutual refinement couples the scales in both directions through space-to-depth feedback, deformable alignment, and per-pixel fusion, so x8 features refine the x2 output. Trained on DF2K, the 7.95M-parameter model achieves a higher PSNR than every compared multi-scale method at x4 and x8 on all five standard benchmarks. At x8, it outperforms the x8-specific DRN-L on all of them, leads all compared methods on Urban100, and is within 0.13 dB of the best result elsewhere. Against three single-scale SwinIR-M models, PMS-SR uses 22% of the parameters, runs 2.9x faster on BSD100 inputs, and its outputs agree 6.7-12.4 dB more closely. Code and pretrained models will be released at https://github.com/julian135707/PMS-SR upon acceptance.

The architecture incorporates a Transformer mechanism for handling low-resolution inputs and utilizes bicubic upsampling as the initial training technique. Subsequently, multiple heads are employed to progressively refine the output, addressing the deficiencies left by lower-resolution scales. In Stage 2, inter-scale refinement techniques such as space-to-depth feedback and deformable alignment are introduced, along with pixel-by-pixel fusion, to enhance the quality of high-resolution features. PMS-SR has been extensively trained on the DF2K dataset, comprising 7.95 million parameters. Experimental results demonstrate superior performance compared to existing single-scale methods, achieving peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) values exceeding those of state-of-the-art single-scale approaches at x4 and x8 across various standard benchmarks. Notably, PMS-SR outperforms the DRN-L model in the x8 benchmark, with a margin of 0.13 dB. Furthermore, when compared to three SwinIR-M single-scale models, PMS-SR exhibits significant advantages in terms of computational efficiency, reducing model size by 22% and enhancing inference speed by 2.9 times on the BSD100 dataset. These improvements are accompanied by a closer alignment of output quality with the SwinIR-M models, with the difference in PSNR scores ranging from 6.7 to 1 dB.

A: Infrared image super-resolution is currently led by Mamba-based networks with 26 to 37 million parameters, which are difficult to deploy on the airborne and handheld platforms where thermal imaging is most needed. This paper presents TIRMamba, a network with 896K to 910K parameters for single-channel thermal imagery. A Thermal Prior Highway computes gradient, local-contrast and spectral cues once at the input and, through one adapter per residual group, modulates a weight-tied bidirectional state-space trunk and gates its dual-scale detail branch; a tri-path reconstruction adds the learned residual to a bicubic radiometric baseline. Because the standard benchmark provides only 265 infrared training images and evaluates fusion products on full images, we train with a replay strategy: grayscale DIV2K pre-training followed by fine-tuning on 64-pixel patches drawn with equal probability from the infrared and natural corpora. At scale factor 4, TIRMamba matches the strongest protocol-trained methods on both official test sets with 29 to 40 times fewer parameters and 2.8 to 9.4 times lower latency; at scale factor 2 it gives the highest SSIM on both. A variant with prior-conditioned selectivity, TIRMamba-Rad, corrects a 3 dB raw-thermal failure of an intermediate size-invariant design and gives the best results at scale factor 4 on raw-thermal, unmanned-aerial-vehicle and independent-sensor test sets. Code and trained models will be released at https://github.com/julian135707/TIRMamba upon acceptance.

A_prime: This study presents the development and evaluation of a lightweight thermal imaging model, TIRMamba, which significantly reduces the computational complexity and memory footprint compared to traditional Mamba networks. Initially designed with parameters ranging from 26 to 37 million bits, the proposed TIRMamba model achieves a compact size of 896K to 910K bits, making it more suitable for real-time applications requiring thermal imaging. The architecture incorporates a Thermal Prior Highway mechanism, leveraging gradient, contrast, and color cues directly from input images. Additionally, a novel two-way state-space trunk composed of adapter modules for each group facilitates efficient processing and feature extraction. To enhance performance, a tri-path combination integrating learned residuals and basic bicubic radiometric adjustments is employed. Given the limited benchmark data consisting of 265 infrared images, the model was pre-trained using grayscale DIV2K images and fine-tuned on 64-pixel chunks randomly selected from both infrared and regular image datasets. The results demonstrate that TIRMamba achieves comparable performance to state-of-the-art protocol-based methods at a zoom level of 4, reducing the number of parameters by 29 to 40 times and decreasing the inference time by 2.8 to 9.4 times. Furthermore, at scale factor 2, TIRMamba exhibits superior structural similarity index measure (SSIM) scores. A specialized variant, TIRMamba-Rad, further improves upon the original model by addressing a 3 dB raw-thermal issue, showcasing its robustness across various scales without compromising its size-agnostic characteristics.

A: Fourier phase encodes important spatial image structure, but recovering an image without measured spectral magnitude requires additional constraints and leaves absolute intensity ambiguous. We propose a projection-based two-stage framework that combines Fourier-phase and spatial-support constraints with an image-specific neural prior. The first stage alternates constraint enforcement with regularized neural-prior updates, while the second performs phase/support refinement alone with guaranteed convergence. We evaluate two neural-prior implementations on the same 77 microscopy images and compare them with a constraint-only baseline. After 500 final refinement passes, the best-performing variant achieves 31.41 dB pooled PSNR, 35.75 dB mean PSNR, and 0.9531 mean SSIM, improving pooled PSNR by 1.51~dB and reducing pooled MSE by 29.3% relative to the baseline. The results demonstrate the benefit of combining neural guidance with explicit constraint refinement at the evaluated iteration budget, while showing that lower phase residual alone does not guarantee greater reconstruction accuracy.

A: Registering a segmented CT to fluoroscopy can locate every fracture fragment but can guide surgery only when trusted. After each shot, our closed loop registers all fragments, bounds their errors with a calibrated sandwich covariance, flags implausible or ambiguous ones, and stops or plans the next view. On simulated fluoroscopy of 60 held-out fracture CTs with realistic image uncertainty, 95% bounds covered 83% of unflagged fragments and 91% of those within 5mm, but from the second view on 14% failed by over 5mm, a third with bounds of at most 2mm. A fragment's shift when a view was added separated tightly bounded failures best (exploratory; AUC 0.94, bound 0.81). Requiring that the newest view moved no fragment beyond its bound, preferred post hoc, lowered false stops at 2mm from 23% to 6% overall, with 345 instead of 362 correct ones but more trajectories uncertified; delaying the stop did not, and other signals at equal acceptance left 10-15% false. With a segmentation error shared by all views (median Dice 0.89), 21% of this rule's stops were false against 10% without it (15 cases; exploratory). Minimax planning certified sooner than the clinical protocol without the check (4.20 versus 4.72 shots, Holm p <0.001), but no criterion reached the pre-specified endpoint, a true 2mm error, significantly sooner, even in the true basin. On real fluoroscopy of five intact pelves no 2mm certificate was false. Trust takes evidence across views, not only a calibrated local bound.

The fragment shift observed when adding a new view revealed that tighter bounds significantly improved performance (exploratory; AUC 0.94, bound 0.81). A_prime: This study focuses on the development and evaluation of a closed-loop registration system for detecting fractures in CT scans during fluoroscopic imaging. The system integrates a series of CT scans to align them with fluoroscopic images, aiming to identify minute fractures accurately. A calibrated sandwich covariance technique is employed to assess registration errors post-each scan, enabling the identification of unreliable fragments. The system flags inconsistencies and provides guidance on subsequent imaging strategies. Testing was conducted using 60 fractured CT scans under simulated fluoroscopic conditions with realistic image uncertainties. Results indicated that the 95% confidence bounds encompassed 83% of flagged fractures and 91% of those within a 5 mm range. However, starting from the second scan, 14% of detected fractures exceeded the 5 mm threshold, and one instance showed bounds less than 2 mm. The performance of the system was further evaluated through Area Under the Curve (AUC) of 0.94 and a bound accuracy rate of 0.81, demonstrating the ability to distinguish reliable from unreliable fractures. By ensuring that new scans did not exceed predefined limits, the system reduced false alarms from 23% to 6%, although this came at the cost of increased uncertainty in subsequent shots. Additionally, the presence of other factors contributing to false positives led to a reduction in false stops to 10% when these additional clues were considered. The study also highlighted the importance of utilizing multiple view perspectives to enhance reliability, noting that even with a median segmentation error of 0.89, some discrepancies persisted. Furthermore, the proposed method significantly accelerated the planning process for imaging sessions, reducing the average number of required shots from 4.72 to 4.20, compared to the standard clinical protocol. Despite the limitations, the system demonstrated potential in improving fracture detection accuracy without achieving the targeted 2 mm error threshold.

A: Source-free domain adaptation (SFDA) is critical for medical image segmentation as it adapts a model to an unlabeled target domain without accessing source data, thereby preserving data privacy. However, its effectiveness is often limited by confirmation bias: self-training models tend to miss small polyps, hallucinate foreground, and produce imprecise contours. We propose MedRT-SFSeg, a real-time SFDA framework built on a dual-head one-to-one/one-to-many YOLO segmentation architecture. Mask-DHF fuses precision- and recall-oriented predictions into stable pseudo-instances, while DURR uses the sign of pixel-level dual-head disagreement as a directional cue to expand or shrink masks, and additionally recovers missed instances and suppresses hallucinations. Seg-MARD further regularizes feature representations through mask-guided, region-stratified sampling. Experiments on bidirectional adaptation between Kvasir-SEG and CVC-ClinicDB show that MedRT-SFSeg achieves 80.43%/80.77% Dice and 5.53/8.44 mm ASD, improving the non-adapted baseline by 7.7 and 9.8 Dice points while running at more than 62 FPS end-to-end. These results suggest that segmentation-aware dual-head supervision can improve pseudo-label quality without sacrificing real-time inference. Project page: https://danielnguyen-05.github.io/MedRT-SFSeg

A_prime: This study explores the application of Spatially-Focused Data Augmentation (SFDA) to enhance medical image segmentation accuracy while prioritizing data privacy. The proposed model, MedRT-SFSeg, integrates a YOLO architecture with dual-head methods to achieve one-to-one and many-to-one segmentations. Utilizing Mask-Dual Head Fusion (Mask-DHF), the model ensures crisp segmentation outcomes by balancing precision and recall. Additionally, Dual-Resolution Relevance (DURR) enhances segmentation performance through adaptive mask size adjustments based on pixel-level dual-head interactions, thereby identifying and eliminating false positives. Further refinement is achieved via Segmentation Mean Average Recall Difference (Seg-MARD), which optimizes feature extraction using generated masks and partitions the segmented regions effectively. Experimental validation was conducted on the Kvasir-SEG and CVC-ClinicDB datasets, demonstrating superior performance compared to existing methods. MedRT-SFSeg achieved Dice coefficients of 80.43% and 80.77% for the Kvasir-SEG and CVC-ClinicDB datasets, respectively, with Average Surface Distance (ASD) metrics reduced to 5.53 and 8.44 mm, respectively. These improvements represent a significant enhancement over previous studies, achieving gains of 7.7 and 9.8 Dice coefficients. Notably, the system operates efficiently at over 62 frames per second (FPS). The findings suggest that the dual-head approach successfully delivers both speed and accuracy without compromising segmentation quality. Detailed information regarding the implementation and experimental results can be found at https://danielnguyen-05.github.io/MedRT-SFSeg.

A: Sub-hourly dispatch, balancing, and storage control increasingly depend on forecasts that anticipate rapid variability in solar generation. Accurate sky-image-based irradiance forecasting requires a combination of visual cloud dynamics with recent irradiance state while adapting to different short-term irradiance-change regimes. To address this, we introduce GateFormer, a GHI-conditioned dual-decoder ViT for intra-hour global horizontal irradiance (GHI) forecasting through forecast-space decomposition. GateFormer embeds observed GHI into the visual token stream, allowing interaction with sky-image patch features through self-attention. From this shared representation, a Trajectory Head predicts future GHI sequence, while a Delta Head predicts final-horizon change from the latest observed GHI. The two final-horizon forecasts are adaptively weighted in prediction space, with magnitude- and direction-supervision targeting the remaining error. On the NREL-TSI benchmark, GateFormer attains 125.01 W/m^2 RMSE at +30 min, improving over a state-of-the-art transformer baseline by 9.6% under paired-timestamp evaluation. Across NREL-TSI, Chilbolton, and SIRTA, GateFormer achieves the lowest final-horizon RMSE among the evaluated baselines, with forecast skill of 22.97-28.86% relative to smart persistence. Component ablations show adaptive weighting outperforms both individual decoders and fixed averaging, distinguishing GateFormer from conventional forecast combination, while the supervised correction further reduces RMSE by 1.68 W/m^2 and MAE by 4.86 W/m^2. Ramp-regime diagnostics show larger gains during operationally important positive ramps, reducing RMSE by 26.27 W/m^2. These results identify forecast-space decomposition as an alternative forecasting formulation, with potential relevance to other multimodal short-horizon forecasting tasks and deployment using only sky images and measured GHI.

A_prime: This study explores the application of image and video processing techniques for solar energy forecasting, specifically focusing on the prediction of hourly Global Horizontal Irradiance (GHI). The proposed method, named GateFormer, is a dual-decoder Vision Transformer (ViT) architecture designed to decompose forecast-space data through a novel approach known as forecast-space decomposition. GateFormer ingests real-time GHI values into a visual token stream, enabling feature extraction from sky-image patches via self-attention mechanisms. This process yields two distinct heads: a Trajectory Head responsible for forecasting future GHI sequences, and a Delta Head for predicting the final-horizon changes based on the most recent GHI readings. By integrating these predictions within the forecast space, GateFormer aims to minimize residual errors. Empirical evaluations conducted on the National Renewable Energy Laboratory - Total Solar Irrigation (NREL-TSI) benchmark demonstrate that GateFormer achieves an outstanding Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) of 125.01 W/m² at a lead time of +30 minutes, surpassing the previously reported state-of-the-art transformers by 9.6%. Moreover, GateFormer exhibits superior performance across various datasets, including NREL-TSI, Chilbolton, and SIRTA, with the lowest RMSE values among all baseline models. A: Cyclist fatality rates remain high despite policy support for active travel, and autonomous vehicles add complexity to mixed traffic. Neither crash statistics nor multi-model detection pipelines scale to continuous monitoring of perceived safety along a route. We present an edge-assisted crowdsensing system: handlebar cameras supply street-level frames, a vision-language model (VLM) turns each frame into structured traffic attributes through a single prompt, and an explainable boosting machine (EBM) combines them with OpenStreetMap road infrastructure and on-bike kinematics to predict a crowdsourced 1-9 safety score. Extraction belongs at the network edge: the fastest self-hosted model needs 2.49 s per frame and scoring takes 0.4 ms on a CPU. On 1,362 annotated frames from two London routes, the EBM regressor reaches 72.2 percent binary accuracy and a mean absolute error of 1.011 under five-fold cross-validation. It is within one accuracy point of black-box ensembles. Its per-feature shape functions give exact attribution: physical lane separation is worth +0.97 rating points, a painted lane +0.70 and a construction site -0.65. Planners can therefore price an infrastructure change in rating points, and the results enter cost-benefit analysis directly. We also report inter-annotator agreement (alpha = 0.4695), an attribute audit, and a sensitivity analysis linking attribute error to accuracy. With re-encoding, a 20 s sampling interval serves 1,000 riders at 54 Mbit/s at a cost of 1.4 accuracy points, making continuous monitoring practical.

A: Automatic extraction and anatomical numbering (R01-R12, L01-L12) of all 24 rib centerlines in thoracic CT is essential for unfolded rib visualization, fracture detection, and surgical navigation, but remains challenging due to adjacent-bone confluence, calcified costal cartilage bridges, kyphotic pose variation, and partial visibility of terminal ribs. We present ribline, an open-source three-stage framework combining: (1) an automatically detected lung-apex and vertebral-midline coordinate frame with a kyphosis-aware azimuthal angle for point ordering along each rib; (2) a hybrid voxel detector fusing an anatomically anchored Semantic Context Forest (SCF) with a lightweight 3D U-Net; and (3) a global stage that decomposes the probability skeleton into candidate curves, assigns rib indices via a bilateral Viterbi dynamic program coupled across both hemithoraces, and refines curves via template recovery and normal-plane centering (RibSnake). On the Siemens Corporate Research 2 mm thoracic CT benchmark (47 training and 12 evaluation scans), our pipeline achieves a labeled Chamfer distance of 2.05 mm, labeled clDice of 0.886 (3 mm) and 0.945 (4 mm), 97.2% labeling accuracy (278/286 ribs), and zero false-positive curves on the evaluation split, and 3.64 mm (median 2.39 mm) with 91.8% labeling accuracy across all 59 annotated scans (1,402 ribs) in 5-fold cross-validation. Code: https://github.com/wq2012/ribline Pretrained Models: https://huggingface.co/collections/wq2012/ribline

A: Humanoid loco-manipulation requires continuous coordination of high-dimensional whole-body motion to realize task objectives. While vision-language-action models and world action models transfer semantic and visual-dynamics priors to robot control, these priors do not necessarily capture the structure of robot motion. We introduce Kinematic Action Models (KAMs), a paradigm that treats whole-body motion as a direct pretraining target and uses a pretrained motion generator as the primary action-generation backbone. KAMs ground learned temporal and cross-body coordination priors through task conditioning, visual observations, and execution feedback. We present Kimodo-Policy as an initial instantiation, combining a frozen Kimodo text-to-motion backbone with lightweight ControlNet-based visual conditioning. A root-body-hand hierarchy coordinates locomotion and manipulation, while motion-history conditioning and repeated action-chunk prediction bridge motion synthesis and closed-loop control. Following large-scale loco-manipulation pretraining, the policy achieves the highest overall success among compared policies on multi-task HumanoidArena (72.14%), competitive performance on SIMPLE, and 60% mean success across eight real-world tasks, with 678M parameters (92M trainable). Ablations support the contribution of the pretrained motion backbone. Together, these results provide initial evidence for motion generation as a complementary foundation for humanoid action learning.

KAMs use learned patterns from past motion, visual stuff, and what happens when actions are actually carried out. We started with Kimodo-Policy, which mixes a set Kimodo motion model with a small-scale visual conditioning system called ControlNet. There's a main part for moving around and another for handling objects. We also look at past movements and make guesses about action chunks for better motion and control. We've pretrained this policy on a big dataset, and it works really well on HumanoidArena (72.14%), does a good job on SIMPLE, and does okay on eight real-life tasks (60%). Our policy has 678 million parameters, but only 92 million need to be trained. Ablations show the value of our motion generator. The policy consists of two main modules: one for movement and another for object handling. These findings suggest that motion generation may serve as a critical step towards enabling humanoid robots to perform complex tasks effectively.

A: Vision-language-action (VLA) models pair a vision-language backbone with an action head, but in closed-loop control the backbone sits on the control-critical path: while it computes, the robot keeps moving, so each executed action is conditioned on an increasingly stale observation. A larger backbone therefore directly blocks reactivity, especially in humanoid dexterous manipulation. We present DASH, a Decoupled Asynchronous System for Humanoids that removes this coupling. DASH splits the policy into a slow vision-language model (System 2) and a fast flow-matching action head (System 1) that run as concurrent processes over the LCM communication protocol, so the control rate is set by the action head alone, independent of backbone size. The action head fuses stale semantics from a frozen backbone with fresh vision from its own ResNet encoder, desynchronized training exposes it to the staleness it meets at deployment, and an adaptive temporal aggregator aligns overlapping action chunks under variable inference latency. On an asynchronous RoboTwin benchmark that charges inference latency in simulated time, DASH holds 20 Hz control rate from 0.8B to 8B backbones while the synchronous rate falls from 9.7 to 4.1 Hz, with higher success at every size. On a real humanoid with dexterous hands, DASH achieves clearly higher pick-and-place success than the synchronous pipeline.

This leads to the robot acting based on outdated information, which can be especially bad for tasks requiring dexterous manipulation. On a RoboTwin benchmark, our setup keeps a 20 Hz control rate even for backbones between 0.8B to 8B, which is much better than the synchronous version that drops from 9.7 to 4.1 Hz. To address this issue, we propose DASH, an innovative decoupled asynchronous system designed specifically for humanoid robots. DASH separates the policy into two distinct components: a slow vision-language model (System 2) and a rapid action head (System 1), both of which operate concurrently through the Lightweight Communication Manager (LCM) protocol. This architecture enables System 1 to maintain control speed irrespective of the size and computational demands of System 2. The action head is trained to manage outdated information and employs a dynamic alignment strategy to synchronize actions with varying latencies. A: Mobile robots operating in homes need reliable 3D perception of nearby furniture and surrounding structures, yet recovering this information on both sides of the robot's path with a single forward-mounted millimeter-wave radar remains challenging because of near-field wavefront curvature, viewpoint-dependent target visibility, and limited elevation diversity. This paper presents a motion-assisted framework for reconstructing structures on both sides of a robot's trajectory. Our near-field model relates scene reflectivity to stepped-frequency multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) observations across frequencies and robot positions using spherical paths from transmitter (Tx) to scatterer to receiver (Rx). Bilateral Tx combining provides wideband directional weighting, while sliding-aperture back-projection coherently focuses the measurements using near-field propagation distances. Top-K power fusion combines local images with different visibility. The reconstruction provides lateral-forward support for multi-layer height extraction, followed by guarded adaptive height refinement using the original MIMO channels. Experiments in controlled, office/study, and corridor environments produce mean lateral-forward localization errors of 4.65, 5.63, and 5.98 cm, respectively, with peak-to-background ratios (PBRs) exceeding 13 dB. The framework recovers bilateral 3D scattering structure from one forward pass using a single radar, without relying on learned representations of the scene.
