A: We show that a hardwired distributed processing unit (HDPU) can take a neural decision at the sensor and so remove the inference from the host. Built for zebra-crossing detection on a low-cost Artix-7 FPGA, the unit decides on every camera frame in a fixed 2,269,477 clock cycles (34.04 ms depends upon Fpga clk ), inside the 37.49-ms frame period, and on the board it returns the same scores and decisions as its bit-exact software model on all 639 test images. The whole detection path, from camera pixels to decision, takes 1,814 LUTs, with no processor, no operating system and no full-resolution frame store. When the unit answers instead of reporting "not sure", 95.7% of its answers on street photographs are correct, and a hardware contrast stage lifts accuracy on camera-like dashcam frames from 47.7% to 78.2%. The host is spared all of the inference: 8.13 ms of a core in every frame period, where a full-precision ResNet-18 would need more than a frame period even on 16 threads. It also receives 16 bytes per frame instead of 614,400, 38,400 times less. The unit is an 80x60-pixel pipeline feeding a four-layer binarized CNN with 93,408 one-bit weights, verified bit-exactly from a Python model through RTL simulation to the board. Earlier HDPUs did pre-processing (edges, corners, steering); this one shows that the decision itself can move to the sensor.

A: Wearable ultrasound enables continuous deep-tissue monitoring, and a single programmable probe can operate in multiple complementary modes, such as structural A-mode and Doppler flow measurement. However, each operating mode requires dedicated measurement parameters and peripheral states, with no single configuration serving all modes on resource-constrained devices. Time multiplexing of operating modes introduces reconfiguration latency that lowers the effective mode repetition rate. To address this limitation, we present an open-source, transition-aware control stack for low-latency, in-session reconfiguration of the 32-channel TinyProbe wearable platform. Operating modes are described as hardware configurations, and host-side shadow registers track the peripheral states, enabling transition-specific register updates. Transition sequences are executed either by the host (over Wi-Fi 6) or by a firmware loop on the probe MCU. We validate the stack on a pulsatile-flow phantom by interleaving blocks of 25 to 100 pulsed-wave Doppler shots at 1.43 kHz PRF with single 16-channel A-mode acquisitions, changing channel configurations at every transition. Compared to full reconfiguration, the overhead per transition decreases from 30.2 ms to 11.6 ms (host-scheduled) and 3.1 ms (MCU-scheduled). For 75-shot Doppler blocks, the multi-mode repetition rate reaches 16.0 Hz (MCU-scheduled), 90.1% of the theoretical maximum of 17.7 Hz. Concurrent reconstruction of a Doppler spectrogram and a lumen-diameter trace demonstrates the functionality of time-multiplexed flow and structural monitoring.

A: AI training and inference workloads make GPU power swing repeatedly between compute and communication phases. As a result, the cascaded converters in a datacenter rack keep moving between operating points with different efficiencies. This paper uses an energy based, cycle averaged method to quantify that effect along a 240 V AC to 400 V DC to 51 V DC rack power path, using measured efficiency curves of commercially available GaN based PFC and LLC converters. For a 1 Hz, 50% duty-cycle load swinging between 5 kW and 510 W, conversion efficiency falls to 95.97%, compared with 96.82% at the equivalent constant average load, a loss of 0.88%. When 51/48V to 1V point of load conversion to the chip rail is included, it is shown that the loss grows to 1.66% (89.45% vs. 90.96%). These results show that efficiency rated at average load overstates real world performance, and that the penalty grows with each load dependent conversion stage between the grid and the GPU.

We used real efficiency curves from commercially available GaN-based PFC and LLC converters. Our findings for a 1 Hz, 50% duty-cycle load that varies from 5 kW to 510 W indicate a conversion efficiency drop to 95.97%, as opposed to 96.82% with a steady average load. This represents a 0.88% loss. When we also consider the conversion from 51/48 V to 1 V right at the chip rail, the loss increases to 1.66% (89.45% vs. 90.96%). These results highlight that efficiency figures often given at average load can misrepresent actual performance in real-world scenarios, and this underestimation becomes more significant with each conversion step between the grid and the GPU.

A: Deploying Vision Transformers (ViTs) on low-power edge devices is challenging due to high computational demands. Conventional pruning frameworks require a separate compiled binary for each sparsity level, increasing storage overhead and limiting runtime adaptability. This paper presents an end-to-end deployment pipeline that transforms pretrained ViTs into a single runtime-configurable binary, enabling dynamic compute-budget switching on embedded CPUs. This is achieved by restructuring generated C kernels with modified loop bounds and binary-mask control logic, allowing execution to switch across discrete sparsity levels via compact external configuration files. Compared to multi-binary deployment, the proposed runtime-adaptive approach reduces on-device storage by up to 4.86x, requiring only 163 MB for ViT-Base instead of nearly 800 MB. To maximize pruning efficiency, we introduce a hardware-aligned block pruning strategy for Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) layers. In addition, a custom ISA extension is proposed to exploit input-reuse patterns in linear projection kernels. On a Synopsys TRV32P3FX RISC-V processor, the full system achieves up to 2.8x speedup at 65% MLP and 50% attention-head pruning for ViT-Base. The ISA extension alone provides a 1.56x speedup and 33% lower inference energy, with a 24.7% area overhead in a TSMC 28 nm implementation.

Compared to multi-binary deployment, the proposed runtime-adaptive approach reduces on-device storage by up to 4.86x, requiring only 163 MB for ViT-Base instead of nearly 800 MB. On a Synopsys TRV32P3FX RISC-V processor, the full system achieves up to 2.8x speedup at 65% MLP and 50% attention-head pruning for ViT-Base. The ISA extension alone provides a 1.56x speedup and 33% lower inference energy, with a 24.7% area overhead in a TSMC 28 nm implementation.

A: LEO satellite networks such as Starlink provide Internet connectivity across continents, oceans, and airspace. IP geolocation providers map Starlink's IPv6 prefixes to locations mainly through its self-published GeoFeed. However, users may be far away from their assigned Points of Presence (PoPs), one label covers an entire prefix, and labels and PoP mappings can change while addresses stay the same. We characterize Starlink's IPv6 addressing using 925 historical GeoFeed snapshots (2024--2026), one year of PoP mappings, and over 7.9 million observed IPv6 addresses. Our findings reveal that customer prefixes lack clear geographic structure, prefix labels lie a median of 540km from their PoPs, and relabeling a single /40 can affect the reported locations of up to 65,536 possible /56 delegations. To address these challenges, we propose StarLoc, a geographic Locator--Identifier separation scheme that embeds terminal location into IPv6 addresses using a resolution-adaptive H3 Locator while preserving existing Starlink prefixes, /56 delegations, and stable Endpoint Identifiers. To balance accuracy and privacy, StarLoc reveals only cells with at least a certain number of terminals, and operators can cap resolution in sensitive regions or withhold location entirely. Unlike topology-based schemes, StarLoc encodes physical location and lets Locators follow moving users.

A: Wi-Fi sensing promises to turn the everyday wireless signals that already surround us into ubiquitous sensors for human sensing. However, a fundamental obstacle is that CSI is acquired under diverse device-specific configurations, including different subcarrier counts, bandwidths, and carrier bands. Consequently, the resulting CSI tensors vary in both spectral resolution and tensor shape, making heterogeneous modeling challenging. Standard architectures struggle with such heterogeneity, forcing lossy pre-processing which compromises the underlying signal. To bridge this gap, we present UniCSI, a unified foundation architecture that directly operates on heterogeneous CSI while preserving the integrity of the native waveform. UniCSI hinges on two core innovations: (1) a physics-informed RF tokenizer that encodes each frequency channel based on its fractional position within the physical spectrum rather than rigid array indices. It preserves intrinsic spectral coherence and enables seamless, frequency resolution-agnostic processing across arbitrary sensing configurations. (2) a spectral aggregator that distills variable-length channel sequences into a fixed-size spectral signature, effectively decoupling the feature dimensionality from the physical subcarrier spacing. Extensive evaluations on a large-scale corpus of 25 heterogeneous public datasets, spanning 14 to 2048 subcarriers, 20 to 160 MHz bandwidth, and the 2.4 and 5 GHz bands, demonstrate that native heterogeneous ingestion substantially improves cross-domain transfer under both supervised and self-supervised training schemes, particularly in regimes where fixed-grid architectures fail to generalize.

This makes it tough to model them because they don't look the same, which messes with our standard tech. That's why we've come up with UniCSI, a new kind of architecture that's built to work directly with this diverse CSI data, keeping the original signal strong and intact. UniCSI's got two key tricks to pull this off. First, there's this new RF tokenizer that uses the actual spectrum positions instead of just counting frequency bins. This way, we keep the original signal quality and can handle different sensor setups with ease. It really shines when compared to old-school architectures, especially when they can't handle the variety in real-world situations. We see a real boost in learning across different domains when we use UniCSI, whether we're using labeled data or just letting the model learn on its own.

A: Early-stage encrypted traffic classifiers make decisions from only the first few packets of a connection, enabling low-latency classification but raising robustness concerns under realistic traffic morphing. Existing adversarial traffic generation methods often assume complete flows, feature-level perturbations, or iterative runtime feedback, which do not match the constraints of early-stage execution. We present NetGuise, a target-conditioned traffic morphing framework that generates packet-level padding and non-negative delay actions while preserving packet direction, ordering, and packet count and respecting MTU, bandwidth, and latency constraints. We evaluate NetGuise for censorship evasion under two observation interfaces, i) a history-only causal interface for online packet-by-packet execution, ii) and a full-window oracle interface that provides an upper-bound characterization of early-stage morphability. On VANT, NetGuise achieves 33.2% mean targeted evasion under the causal interface versus 82.0% under the oracle interface; on UTMobileNet, the corresponding results are 5.6% and 81.8%. NetGuise outperforms the strongest causal baseline, BAP, on both datasets and, on VANT, reduces bandwidth overhead from 19.80% to 3.02% and generation latency from 37.42 ms/flow to 1.16 ms/flow. Under the oracle interface, it achieves up to 85.7% targeted evasion, retains 43.5% after four rounds of adaptive censor retraining, and maintains 48% under zero-shot cross-environment transfer. Our results show that early-stage classifiers can remain morphable despite high clean accuracy and that robustness evaluation should account for targeted morphability, observation constraints, defender adaptation, and operational network conditions.

That's why we developed NetGuise, a new way to change packet traffic that adds padding and manages delays without messing up packet direction, order, or number. We also made sure it doesn't break MTU, bandwidth, or latency limits. We tested NetGuise on VANT and UTMobileNet, and it did a pretty good job at getting past censors. On VANT, it managed to slip past censors 33.2% of the time with just a history of what happened, and 82.0% when we had a full view. On UTMobileNet, it was 5.6% and 81.8% respectively. Not only that, but it did better than the best causal baseline, BAP, and it made the network use less bandwidth (from 19.80% to 3.02%) and reduced the time it took to generate traffic (from 37.42 ms/flow to 1.16 ms/flow). A: Securing bandwidth-constrained Internet of Things (IoT) and edge networks during post-quantum migration creates an authentication trade-off: ML-KEM provides post-quantum key establishment, whereas post-quantum signatures increase certificate-chain size, verification cost, and handshake latency. We present HPQ-AKE, a sign-less hybrid authenticated key exchange for RSA-enabled IoT gateways and edge/cloud services that replaces transcript signatures with dual KEMs. HPQ-AKE combines ML-KEM-768 for post-quantum session secrecy and forward secrecy with RSA-OAEP for implicit mutual authentication, preserving existing RSA-enabled infrastructure during migration. We analyze HPQ-AKE in an extended Bellare-Rogaway model, separating classical authentication in the Random Oracle Model from session-key secrecy in the Quantum Random Oracle Model. Under the Module-LWE and RSA assumptions, it establishes AKE security, forward secrecy, and conditional KCI resistance under the long-term-key-only exposure assumptions. Evaluation combines x86 micro-benchmarking, analytical latency modeling, and 10,000-iteration Monte Carlo simulation. HPQ-AKE reduces modeled handshake transmission from 13,009 to 5,668 Bytes, a 56.4% reduction relative to a Hybrid TLS 1.3 Full handshake, while requiring 7.11 ms of total local computation on the measured x86 testbed. Under a simulated 50 kbps satellite-like link with 600 ms RTT and stochastic jitter, median latency is 1,914 ms, 31.4% below the 2,791 ms baseline. At 20 ms RTT, modeled break-even thresholds are 0.31 Mbps against the pre-cached baseline and 4.08 Mbps against the full baseline; both decrease as RTT increases. These x86-based results motivate evaluation on gateway-class IoT and edge platforms; performance on ARM gateways and unaccelerated microcontrollers remains unvalidated.

Specifically, we replace traditional heavy transcript signatures with a combination of two key encapsulation mechanisms (KEMs): the ML-KEM-768 for post-quantum key secrecy and forward secrecy, and RSA-OAEP for secure mutual identity verification. Our investigation encompasses aspects of authenticated key exchange (AKE) security, forward secrecy, and resistance to known-plaintext attacks (KCI). To rigorously evaluate the efficacy of HPQ-AKE, we conducted extensive testing using x86 architecture, including detailed analytical timing studies and a Monte Carlo simulation involving 10,000 iterations. These tests demonstrate that HPQ-AKE outperforms its predecessor by reducing the message size from 13,009 bytes to 5,668 bytes, achieving a significant reduction in overhead. Furthermore, the computational efficiency of our method is noteworthy, with a local processing time of only 7.11 milliseconds. When considering a simulated 50 kilobits per second (kbps) link with a 600 millisecond round-trip time (RTT), our median processing time is reduced to 1,914 milliseconds, thereby significantly diminishing the baseline time of 2,791 milliseconds. Importantly, the break-even points for achieving these improvements are 0.31 Mbps and 4.08 Mbps at a 20 ms RTT, with these values improving further with increased RTT durations. A: Reliable low-latency connectivity for real-time applications is a key requirement for 5G and future 6G non-terrestrial networks. Low Earth Orbit satellites enable global coverage but impose long propagation delays, rapid channel variations, and delayed feedback, which challenge conventional link adaptation algorithms designed for terrestrial networks. To address this problem, the paper proposes a Multi-Level Outer-Loop Link Adaptation (ML-OLLA) algorithm that assigns a dedicated target block error rate and an independent adaptation process for each transmission attempt. With ML-OLLA, early transmission attempts use higher-rate modulation and coding schemes (MCSs), while later ones use more robust MCSs. The core contribution of this work is a low-complexity data-driven parameter selection method that determines ML-OLLA parameters. Numerical results obtained with ns-3 show that the proposed ML-OLLA algorithm increases the system capacity by up to four times and reduces the minimum supported latency budget. In particular, for the 99.9% reliability target, ML-OLLA reduces the minimum supported latency budget from 60 ms to 40 ms compared with the baseline OLLA.

A: Integrated Access and Backhaul (IAB) is a key enabler for cost-effective millimeter-wave (mmWave) densification, yet practical deployments are strongly constrained by the spatial availability of fiber-connected IAB donors. Variations in donor topologies reshape both the initial coverage footprint and the feasible multi-hop backhaul expansion patterns, causing planning policies trained on a single topology to generalize poorly. This paper studies cross-topology generalization for resilience-aware IAB deployment under coverage and transport feasibility requirements. We formulate IAB deployment as a constrained Markov decision process that couples access coverage satisfaction with multi-hop transport feasibility, including hop-by-hop rate-budget degradation and a minimum parent-connectivity requirement for fault tolerance. To solve the resulting large discrete planning problem, we propose a graph-based actor-critic approach that uses a Graph Attention Network v2 (GATv2) encoder with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), and we develop a multi-stage curriculum learning strategy that progressively increases constraint difficulty and scenario diversity for stable training and transferable policies. In a 60 GHz urban simulation over a 1000 m x 1000 m area with multiple donor layouts, the trained policy satisfies the minimum coverage requirement of 98% with fewer deployed IAB nodes than learning and heuristic baselines, and maintains higher coverage under progressive backhaul failures. The results demonstrate that curriculum-trained graph-based reinforcement learning can improve deployment efficiency and resilience while transferring across heterogeneous IAB donor topologies without retraining.

A: Mobile latency is determined by how Mobile Network Operators (MNOs) route traffic: from phones, across the MNO's network to exit points where it enters the public Internet. Exit points are few, and MNOs are quiet about details, but their role prompts us to ask: What is the latency cost of sending traffic through an exit point? We develop a new method to evaluate this question, and demonstrate it on the three largest U.S. MNOs, although in principle it can apply globally. Using new analysis of existing traceroutes, we find that AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon funnel nationwide traffic through only 9, 5, and 9 exits, and the geographic detour they incur adds up to 62.1 ms compared to an ideal, direct-path latency. Routing delays also add latency. We show that even assuming speed-of-light paths through the exit points, latency is still up to 46.9 ms more than optimal. To understand if these costs can be overcome, we compare actual to theoretically optimal placements, finding that the latencies of current placements are 18-66% above the population-weighted optimum and 32-72% above the market-share-weighted optimum with the same number of exits. However, we show this gap is small in absolute terms: perfect placement would recover only a few milliseconds of the tens that remain. We show that geographic optimization saves little latency: the inflation users experience comes from routing and other overhead.

This article proposes a mission-critical communications system supporing Mission Critical Push-to-Talk (MCPTT), Mission Critical Video (MCVideo), and Mission Critical Data (MCData) over a private 5G standalone network with Non-Terrestrial Network (NTN) connectivity. A context-aware Quality, Priority, and Pre-emption (QPP) mechanism is proposed to dynamically adapt network resource allocation according to the operational state of Mission Critical Services (MCX). Extensions to the Open5GS Policy Control Function (PCF) and Session Management Function (SMF) enable priority and pre-emption updates for existing flows without session re-establishment. The architecture supports tactical edge deployment of service and media functions while retaining centralized service control. Experimental evaluation considers three configurations: terrestrial backhaul with centralized media processing, satellite backhaul with centralized media processing, and satellite backhaul with edge media processing. Results show that tactical edge processing reduces communication delay and packet loss. Under satellite backhaul, edge processing reduced the 95th-percentile MCPTT audio transport delay by 60.03 ms and packet loss by 9.42 percentage points, while achieving a 95th-percentile MCPTT access time of 184.52 ms. These findings demonstrate the benefits of tactical edge media processing and provide an experimental foundation for context-aware priority mechanisms in public-safety networks integrating terrestrial and non-terrestrial components.
I: In this study, we look at how public mobile networks can go down during disasters, making it hard for emergency services to communicate. We're suggesting a special communication system that can handle Mission Critical Push-to-Talk (MCPTT), Mission Critical Video (MCVideo), and Mission Critical Data (MCData) over a private 5G network that also uses Non-Terrestrial Network (NTN) connections. Our idea includes a Quality, Priority, and Pre-emption (QPP) system that changes how network resources are used based on what the emergency services need. We made some changes to the Open5GS PCF and SMF so that existing communication can get these updates without starting over. The design allows us to set up service functions on the edge and still manage them from a central location. We tested three different setups: one with a regular mobile backhaul and central media handling, another with a satellite backhaul and central media handling, and the last one with a satellite backhaul but with media processed at the edge. Our tests showed that processing at the edge helps decrease the time it takes to send messages and reduces the loss of data packets. Specifically, when using the satellite backhaul with edge processing, the MCPTT audio transport delay got cut by about 60.03 ms, and packet loss went down by 9.42%. Also, the MCPTT access time dropped to 184.52 ms. Our work helps show how better edge media processing can improve communications in emergency networks that mix on-ground and NTN resources.

A: Perimeter triage faces a latency/semantics trade-off: signature engines are fast and format-safe but blind to unseen attacks, while generative models are semantic but slow and unparseable. We present VX-One, a small multi-head network (100K--10M parameters) with calibrated typed outputs: a binary gate, a closed-set choice with an explicit unknown option where the benchmark supports it (and abstention elsewhere), and an ordinal score. Heads are temperature-calibrated, with 0.7--1.7 ms single-event CPU p50 latency. We evaluate UNSW-NB15, CIC-IDS2017, and EMBER2024 against calibrated XGBoost, Random Forest, MLP, and Kitsune baselines, and measure a Suricata-to-VX-One cascade over five days of CIC-IDS2017. Results are deliberately double-sided: on UNSW the gate ties the best baseline (0.9837+/-0.0002 versus MLP 0.9835+/-0.0013 across three seeds), while VX-One wins temporal CIC detection (0.734+/-0.022 versus 0.639+/-0.027) but loses multi-class attribution to XGBoost. Under leave-one-family-out, the gate detects all nine UNSW families but drops below chance on CIC recon; CIC trees transfer better. Suricata resolves only about 0.1% of attacks on flow reconstructions and 0.2--2.2% on payload-bearing PCAPs; the strictly by-day Phase 2 recovers only the in-scope DoS/DDoS share on the wave day (recall 0.34, precision 0.97). Calibration collapses under temporal drift (ECE 0.04->0.40) for every method while ranking partly survives. We contribute a measured account of where typed calibrated decisions help perimeter triage, and where they fail.

A: Radio access network (RAN) telemetry reveals radio conditions, protocol behavior, and their consequences for applications. Evaluating its usefulness requires controlled impairments and observations of the same execution. We present C and Python channel brokers and a fault injection workflow for software 5G testbeds connecting an OCUDU base station and a software UE through ZeroMQ. The brokers apply scheduled, directional transformations to I/Q samples and restore the link, while the workflow jointly records applied faults, native and programmable (codelet) telemetry, and application delay. We demonstrate this capability through 45 comparative trials of brief uplink interruptions and stepped additive noise. These use cases distinguish recognizing a radio change from measuring its service consequence: native missing-feedback events retrospectively identify interruptions, whereas noise changes decoding-error measurements without producing those events. Median on-time round-trip times remain near 30 ms, but the prespecified comparisons show mean increases in on-time 95th-percentile delay of 354 and 604 ms for one and five interruptions, and 113 ms for noise. Adding receive-side radio link control (RLC) codelet summaries did not improve interruption classification on held-out trials. The framework provides a reusable way to evaluate measurement choices under known radio faults, before using them in monitoring or learning systems.

The fault injection workflow we've established captures the faults, both native and programmable telemetry, and the delays experienced by applications. We ran 45 tests with quick uplink interruptions and stepped-up additive noise, showing differences in identifying radio condition changes versus the impact on services. The average round-trip times were close to 30 ms, but increased on-time 95th-percentile delay averages were 354 ms for a single interruption, 604 ms for five, and 113 ms for noise. Adding in RLC codelet summaries didn't enhance our ability to identify interruptions when tested with new data. A: Antenna diversity in Internet of Things (IoT) devices is explored to address challenges associated with fixed device orientation and interference from nearby metallic objects, which can degrade wireless network performance. Integrating multiple antennas with different polarizations can significantly enhance signal quality and network reliability. Experiments demonstrated significant improvements in link quality, with gains exceeding 30 dB in received signal strength for specific scenarios. Already the addition of a second PCB-based antenna alone, resulted in a 17 dB improvement. These findings suggest that the added complexity in hardware and software to incorporate antenna diversity could well be justified by the resulting enhancements in network stability for real-world applications.

A: 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) enables high-quality real-time novel-view synthesis for dynamic scenes, supporting free-viewpoint video, mobile XR, and autonomous systems at the edge. Methods using explicit 4D distributions, keyframe interpolation, or anchor binding share two GPU data-movement bottlenecks. Temporal filtering follows model record loading, wasting LPDDR5 bandwidth on inactive data. Frame-isolated execution also overlooks highly overlapping active sets and depth relationships across adjacent frames, reloading shared attributes when working sets exceed on-chip cache capacity. To address these bottlenecks, we present GSPIM, a temporal-locality-aware 4DGS accelerator for PIM-enabled edge devices. Polymorphic PIM adapts a shared near-memory datapath to representation-specific field layouts and selection procedures. It filters and compacts valid data into contiguous inputs before the GPU accesses complete attributes, reducing ineffective transfers. Multi-Frame Rendering Dataflow reuses active attributes and stable depth relationships within a temporal window, reducing repeated work across frames. Hybrid Dataflow Scheduling overlaps near-memory data preparation with GPU rendering to reduce waiting. Evaluation combines a GPU-PIM model calibrated to Jetson AGX Orin 64 GB with a 1z DRAM physical implementation of the added circuits. Across three 4DGS methods and six dynamic scenes, GSPIM achieves a 4.15x geometric-mean speedup and a 4.99x geometric-mean energy-efficiency improvement over a fully optimized frame-by-frame GPU baseline. The maximum scene-level PSNR difference is 0.011 dB, and the added physical footprint is 18.7172 square millimeters across 32 LPDDR5 dies.

A: We present a real-time, hybrid framework for occlusion handling and depth-aware tracking in minimally invasive surgeries (MIS). Occlusions caused by surgical instruments often obscure the region of interest (ROI), affecting surgical precision. To address this, our approach integrates enhanced You Only Look Once (YOLO) based detection, Particle Filtering (PF), and monocular depth estimation using Multiple Depth Estimation Accuracy with Single Network (MiDaS). Occlusion is detected using a distance-based threshold between instruments and ROI. Experimental results demonstrate robust instrument detection with a confidence score of 0.85, effective occlusion event handling, and accurate depth prediction with an MAE of 0.34 cm and RMSE of 0.53 cm. Independent phantom-based validation against stereo depth measurements yielded an MAE of 0.65 cm and RMSE of 0.66 cm. The framework further achieved an occlusion detection accuracy of 81.95\% while maintaining real-time performance at 38.7 FPS. Preliminary surgeon feedback indicates that the proposed visualization framework is clinically relevant and holds promise for future intraoperative image-guided navigation and decision support in MIS.

A: Synapse-resolution fruit-fly (Drosophila) connectomes enable neuron-by-neuron simulation of entire insect nervous systems, yet whole-brain models still require computationally demanding software or multiple neuromorphic chips, and single FPGAs support only small or statistical networks. Scaling to the full connectome, per-synapse spike expansion scales queue traffic with fan-out up to 11.2k, while 41-bit neuron states require 6.83 Mbit, exceeding the 6.27 Mbit on-chip block static RAM (BSRAM) of the target device. FPGAFly runs the 166.7k-neuron, 25.6M-connection leaky integrate-and-fire male central nervous system (CNS) connectome on one FPGA. Order-preserving deferred expansion queues one 64-bit descriptor per spike in source-ID order, cutting external memory traffic by 54.5%-57.9% and peak queue data by 95.6%-96.5% with bit-identical results. A 24-bit encoding shares codewords across normal, refractory, and quantized out-of-range states, reducing BSRAM usage from 438 to 270 with 1245 extra LUTs and zero changes across 10,000 MNIST predictions. At 80 MHz on a Gowin GW5AST-LV138, each 100 ms window finishes in 86.83 ms on average and within 93.05 ms across 2000 tests, realizing the first complete Drosophila CNS connectome simulation on one FPGA.

A: Reliable multipath detection is essential for millimeter-wave simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM), where propagation paths reflecting off the environment provide geometric constraints beyond the dominant line-of-sight component. This paper develops constant false alarm rate (CFAR)-based detectors for beam-swept bistatic integrated sensing and communications (ISAC). Starting from conventional CFAR on the I/Q datacube, we derive a modified detector for non-coherently integrated angular power maps, where the post-integration noise statistics differ from those assumed by standard cell-averaging CFAR. To improve practicality, we introduce a multi-cell cell-under-test formulation and a plus-shaped training window that reduces computational cost while accounting for sidelobe structure. The proposed methods are evaluated on experimental 60 GHz indoor measurements using a snapshot-SLAM estimator. Compared with a singular value decomposition (SVD)-based detector, the proposed CFAR approaches reduce the overall positioning RMSE from 0.30 m to 0.24-0.26 m, with the largest improvement in non-line-of-sight snapshots. The multi-cell non-coherent detector further lowers the computational complexity without degrading positioning accuracy, demonstrating its suitability for practical multipath radio-SLAM.

Traditionally, CFAR is applied to the In-phase (I) and Quadrature (Q) data cube, which is subsequently coherently integrated. This departure from conventional practices necessitates a reevaluation of the statistical properties of post-integration noise, which differ significantly from those observed in standard cell-averaging CFAR methodologies. This improvement is particularly pronounced in scenarios involving non-line-of-sight (NLOS) conditions. Furthermore, the integration of multi-cell non-coherent detection further optimizes computational requirements without compromising positional precision, thereby substantiating its applicability and practicality for multipath radio-SLAM applications.

A: Analog flows from specifications to a signed-off layout rarely run without manual iteration. Recent large language model (LLM) agents size circuits with optimizer loops over the device dimensions and stop at the schematic. We present OPERA (OPamp design by an Expert-taught Reasoning Agent), in which a general-purpose LLM agent designs CMOS opamps from specifications to post-layout sign-off with open-source tools. First, the designer teaches the agent the gm/ID method: map the specifications to transconductances and minimum currents, choose gm/ID per device role from characterized lookup tables, and size from equations, leaving a few knobs to search and an explainable design. Second, the agent learns the gLayout framework and taught layout practice, and writes a reusable layout generator that closes the layout and extraction loop at designer-approved gates. In SKY130, the agent designed a shared constant-gm bias and six opamps (5T, folded-cascode and telescopic OTAs; Miller, folded-cascode and telescopic two-stage) for fun >= 50 MHz, PM >= 60 degrees, SR 25 V/μs into 1 pF and a minimum dc gain of 30 to 60 dB. All six layouts are DRC-clean and LVS-matched, and their extracted netlists meet every target at all 15 PVT corners ( fun >= 53.7 MHz, PM >= 62.1 degrees, SR >= 27.9 V/μs). The benchmark netlists are released at https://github.com/AMPICLab/AMPICBench.

A: In this work we look to neuromorphic computing to solve the power consumption problem that audio denoising neural networks face on edge devices like smartphones, wireless headphones and hearing aids. Spiking neural networks (SNNs) have the potential to solve this problem due to their high activation sparsity and low complexity, however many SOTA SNNs require hardware that supports a mixture of operations to be able to fully perform inference. To solve this problem, we convert SOTA audio denoising neural network Spiking-FullSubNet to a hardware friendly version showing that via QAT and activation function simplification we can achieve $\approx28\times$ improvement in power consumption to 52.9nJ per 32ms audio frame when calculated for custom digital hardware in a 45nm process node. We then propose a digital circuit which by means of a sparsity-aware flexible PE array can perform inference of the heterogeneous compute load of Spiking-FullSubNet, and validate this circuit on a PYNQ-Z1 FPGA achieving a real-time factor of 0.727 at 100MHz.

A: This paper presents a scalable distributed acoustic surveillance system for real-time gunshot detection and localiza tion in large-area, GNSS-challenged environments. The system consists of multiple low-cost MEMS microphone array units (MAUs) deployed as distributed anchors. Each MAU performs edge-level sound-event detection using a lightweight Sound De tection and Echo Suppression (SDES) algorithm, followed by a TinyML-based classifier for gunshot identification. For detected gunshots, an enhanced Generalized Cross-Correlation (eGCC) al gorithm estimates intra-array time differences of arrival (TDoAs) with improved robustness under low signal-to-noise ratio and re verberant conditions. Angle-of-arrival (AoA) estimates obtained from individual MAUs are fused through a modified SCO-EV localization framework to determine the gunshot position in a global coordinate system. A misplacement calibration (MC) algorithm compensates for platform orientation errors, improv ing angular consistency and localization accuracy in practical field conditions. Extensive experiments conducted over coverage areas ranging from 4,985 m2 to 49,063 m2 demonstrate reliable operation across varying spatial scales. The proposed framework achieves a Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) of 0.70 for gunshot recognition and average localization errors below 6.5 m over 25,000 m2 , while maintaining errors under 15 m at larger scales. The results demonstrate the practical potential of the proposed system for distributed gunshot surveillance in GNSS challenged large areas.

A channel-recovery framework is derived that enables passive anchors to reconstruct a channel response suitable for super-resolution delay estimation, allowing multipath-robust ranging without participating in a two-way exchange. Coarse arrival-time information is further used to bound the position estimate and reject inconsistent range solutions. Simulation results in modeled indoor environments show that RA-PDoA reduces the 90th-percentile localization error from 175.3 cm to 95.5 cm under body shadowing while maintaining an airtime requirement independent of the number of anchors. A: Programmable receivers allow an optimal performance in the variable conditions of the wireless channel. An extensive analysis of their noise-power trade-off enables the development of a main receiver with embedded wake-up circuitry. This makes the seamless integration of wake-up receivers (WuRXs) in RF receivers possible, avoiding power, area, complexity, and cost overheads in the system. In this paper, we propose the first LoRa-compatible receiver with an integrated wake-up mode and a programmable noise-power trade-off. In main-receiver mode, it consumes 4.57 mW for a sensitivity of -138 dBm, but it can save up to 62.6% of power consumption at the cost of an 8.3-dB sensitivity degradation. In wake-up mode, sensitivity down to -126 dBm is achieved for a 32-ms latency and 1.5 mW of power consumption. The power consumption remains relatively high due to a sub-optimal design of the the phase-locked loop (PLL). In the end, the wake-up mode consumes 3X less than the lowest-noise configuration in main-receiver mode.

A: Bit-interleaved coded modulation (BICM) is widely used in multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) wireless systems. However, separating MIMO data detection from channel decoding and only exchanging per-bit soft information discards correlation information among the bits within each transmit vector. We show that the resulting information loss limits the performance of practical one-shot receivers. Even though iterative detection and decoding (IDD) can recover most of this loss, IDD significantly increases receiver complexity and latency. In order to reduce this loss, we propose COrrelation-Informed Logits (COIL), a soft-output format that combines per-bit soft information with pairwise coupling logits for correlated bits. We show how to incorporate these coupling logits into a conventional belief-propagation-based channel decoder, which enables correlation-aware decoding in a one-shot receiver without IDD. We evaluate COIL in a MIMO-BICM system with a conventional low-density parity-check code. For a 4x4 MIMO orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) system, a one-shot linear minimum mean-square error (LMMSE) receiver with COIL outperforms a conventional one-shot unbiased LMMSE receiver by 1.3dB and operates within 0.8dB of four-iteration IDD, while requiring only a single pass through the data detector.

A: Wireless digital twins enable network policies to be evaluated before deployment, but reproducing channel effects within a running protocol stack requires continuous waveform processing under strict timing constraints. We present MIRAGE, a GPU-accelerated channel emulator that applies propagation effects directly to in-phase and quadrature samples exchanged by software 5G New Radio stacks. MIRAGE combines batched multiuser, multiantenna filtering with timestamped shared-memory transport and radio-driver integrations for OpenAirInterface and OCUDU. External propagation models supply channel responses asynchronously, while versioned buffers ensure consistent coefficients within each processing interval. Experiments on one NVIDIA H100 GPU evaluate waveform accuracy, processing time, channel updates, and full-stack traffic delivery. At 61.44 million samples per second, eight single-antenna links, four two-by-two links, and one four-by-four link meet the tested 0.5 ms bidirectional processing criterion. Waveform errors remain within one integer quantization step per component, with no mixed coefficient versions across 16.7 million analyzed slots. Integration with the X5G testbed enables slice resource allocations to be evaluated before deployment. Both evaluated slices ultimately satisfy their throughput caps, requiring one physical reconfiguration under line-of-sight conditions and four under non-line-of-sight conditions. These results demonstrate full-stack policy evaluation and expose prediction errors affecting transfer to a physical network.

A: Direct-to-device (D2D) satellite systems, particularly those based on 3GPP-compliant non-terrestrial networks (NTN), deliver connectivity to standard mobile phones and IoT devices using terrestrial International Mobile Telecommunications (IMT) spectrum. This raises the risk of harmful cross-border interference into incumbent terrestrial IMT networks, an issue considered under Agenda Item 1.13 of the ITU World Radiocommunication Conference 2027 (WRC-27). This paper presents an ITU-R-compliant assessment of aggregate downlink interference from two hypothetical D2D systems operating in Jordan and Iraq into terrestrial IMT user equipment (UE) in Saudi Arabia, operating in the 698-960 MHz band. Unlike prior studies that evaluate a few test points near a simplified ideal tri-border intersection, we distribute multiple victim UEs along realistic national borders within various strips at a distance of 0-40 km from the borders. We compare two satellite selection strategies: highest-elevation and random strategies. A: Reflected paths can support localization when line-of-sight (LoS) links are blocked, but their usefulness depends on how accurately the stored model predicts their directions. This paper develops electromagnetic-twin (ET) direction-of-arrival (DoA) localization with a persistent, physically calibrated path-angle field. A nominal floor plan supplies virtual-path geometry, and sparse reference probes at known positions learn a compact directional correction. Field order and regularization are selected from calibration data alone. For each user, unordered DoAs are processed by joint position estimation and one-to-one path association, using assignment-aware multistart search and robust Gauss--Newton refinement. New trusted probes update the stored correction through recursive least squares (RLS), without reprocessing all previous measurements. The analysis establishes calibration rank conditions, objective descent, and conditional information gains from reflected paths, while also distinguishing the decay of initialization bias from the convergence of localization error. Synthetic experiments use 500 queries per operating point. At 50% LoS blockage and $1.5^\circ$ DoA error, the calibrated ET achieves 0.39 m root-mean-square error, versus 0.55 m for nominal geometry. After a wall change, its final error is 0.43 m, versus 0.63 m for a frozen calibrated map. Equal-evidence comparisons show competitive calibrated alternatives and faster abrupt-change recovery with sliding-window updates than with the configured RLS. The results support reusable directional calibration, not a universally superior map or update rule, and validation is limited to synthetic first-order reflections with trusted calibration labels.

A: This paper presents xCHEM, a radio-frequency channel emulator that inserts programmable channels between physical radios using a single NI USRP X4xx software-defined radio. External channel models stream impulse responses to its field-programmable gate array without firmware changes or interruption of signal processing. A streaming datapath implements six independently configurable directional channels across four radio interfaces. Each channel uses a sparse finite impulse response filter whose memory-backed delays decouple delay span from multiplier resources. The real and complex variants support 32 and 16 nonzero taps, respectively, with a maximum delay of 16666.62 ns and 4.069 ns resolution. Coefficient scaling and arithmetic right shifts control attenuation. Hardware measurements show root-mean-square errors of 9.5 ps in delay over the full span and 0.11 dB in attenuation. Multipath delays are recovered within one sample. An FPGA coefficient engine produces tested Doppler shifts from +/-1 Hz to +/-1 MHz with mean frequency errors below 0.032 Hz relative to quantized commands after carrier-offset calibration; at 200 Hz, it reduces the measured near-carrier spur by 53.3 dB compared with 1 kHz host updates.

A: Wireless foundation models learn reusable representations across tasks, configurations, and deployment environments. Their pretraining requires environmental breadth, yet wireless datasets often sample few sites densely. We introduce Channels4World, a scene-centered dataset of 100,000 distinct outdoor RF scenes and a procedural method for generating them. Each scene links a generated environment and RF material assignments to 32 base-station (BS) positions, 16,384 UE positions, and aligned variable-length multipath and ordered interaction records at 3.5 and 7~GHz. The corpus comprises 52.43 billion physical BS-UE pairs, 104.86 billion frequency-specific evaluations, and a 29.14-TB packaged payload. Scene identity aligns geometry, placements, channels, and interactions across frequencies, allowing environmental breadth and within-scene observation density to vary independently. The public release offers predefined subsets at multiple scales and separate access to corpus components. A deterministic 90K/10K scene-level train-test split keeps both frequencies and all scene components together. We characterize morphology, RF materials, and transceiver placement across three generation profiles. Controlled propagation and path-retention analyses show that diffraction materially affects retained-link availability and multipath structure, while the retention policy reduces storage substantially with little loss in represented aggregate power. Under matched training exposure, models trained on broader scene collections perform better on held-out scenes, although an equal-episode control shows that scene count alone cannot explain the gain. By making environmental breadth explicit and controllable, Channels4World supports the development and evaluation of wireless foundation models for generalization across deployment environments.

A: Future wireless systems for indoor applications are expected to extend their operating frequencies from sub-6 GHz to mid-band and millimeter wave (mmWave) frequencies to support higher data rates. To characterize the frequency-dependent propagation behavior across these bands, multi-band channel measurements are essential. In this work, we conduct double-directional multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) channel measurements in an indoor environment to enable a consistent comparison across three frequency bands. Measurements are performed using a 16x16 MIMO configuration at center frequencies of 2.55 GHz, 12.75 GHz and 25.5 GHz, covering both line-of-sight (LOS) and obstructed line-of-sight (OLOS) conditions. The measured channels are processed using the space-alternating generalized expectation maximization (SAGE) algorithm to extract multipath parameters, which are subsequently used to characterize the angular power distributions across the three frequency bands. The results show substantial angular-domain similarity across all three bands in both LOS and OLOS conditions, while also highlighting frequency-dependent variations.

A: Semantic error control coding (SECC) can correct the residual errors of a standard channel code with a foundation model that supplies a prior on the source content, but existing SECC schemes are designed for text. In this paper, we develop SECC for image transmission with spatial token interleaving and a two-pass belief propagation (BP) schedule. At the transmitter, a vector-quantized (VQ) tokenizer converts an image into tokens, which are transmitted in multiple low-density parity-check (LDPC) code blocks of fifth-generation New Radio (5G NR). In raster order, a block that BP fails to decode corrupts consecutive token rows, so the interleaver reorders the tokens such that adjacent tokens are carried by different blocks, without additional transmitted bits. At the receiver, after the first BP pass, token recovery fuses the token probabilities given by BP with the predictions of the autoregressive model Emu3-Gen, and the second BP pass decodes each block again with the fused distributions as priors on the information bits. On Kodak24 at 0.5 channel uses per pixel and a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of 0.15 dB, the second pass removes 92% of the token errors left by token recovery, and interleaving reduces the final token error rate by 88%. At medium to high SNR, the proposed receiver exceeds deep joint source--channel coding baselines with the same channel uses by at least 1.2 dB in peak signal-to-noise ratio.

A: We design and evaluate a site-specific neural receiver for the 5G New Radio (NR) uplink. A corridor digital twin built from a radar scan and refined manually provides 28,671 ray-traced channel records for training an eight-round convolutional graph neural network with pilot-aware inputs and auxiliary channel supervision. The GPU on NVIDIA DGX Spark evaluates time--frequency convolutions in parallel across the received grid to accelerate inference. The receiver uses the standard NR uplink waveform and reference signals and feeds soft bits to the existing transport-block decoder. In over-the-air tests with NI USRP B210 radios under common radio settings, the site-trained receiver achieves the highest mean uplink rate at all five positions. At a non-line-of-sight corner, it reaches 16.2 Mb/s, compared with 4.1 Mb/s for the conventional receiver and 2.4 Mb/s for the 3GPP-trained neural receiver. These results demonstrate the feasibility of integrating neural reception into the 5G NR physical layer and show its potential for AI-RAN deployments.

A: Music source separation extracts vocals and instruments from a mixed recording, enabling remixing, content production, and music analysis. Existing systems commonly operate on waveforms or full-band spectrograms. Waveform inputs contain many samples even in short segments, whereas a single spectrogram resolution imposes a shared time-frequency resolution trade-off across frequency ranges. We propose SubRoFormer, a Transformer-based system comprising a subband module and a residual RoFormer module. The subband module decomposes the mixture into frequency-localized, lower-rate signals for separation. It then reconstructs the target waveforms from the estimated subbands. The residual RoFormer module models temporal and cross-band relationships on temporally compressed features. It combines this context with fine-rate features through gated residual fusion to estimate source-specific complex masks. On the MUSDB18-HQ test set, training only on MUSDB18-HQ yields an average signal-to-distortion ratio (SDR) of 10.63 dB across four stems using target-specific models, achieving state-of-the-art performance among the compared systems without extra training data. With 500 additional training songs, a single model jointly separating all four stems achieves an average SDR of 11.59 dB, establishing state-of-the-art performance among the compared single-model multi-stem systems trained with extra data. Code and checkpoints are released at https://github.com/ArchiMickey/SubRoformer.

A: Repeatable test setups support the development and evaluation of integrated sensing and communications (ISAC) hardware and algorithms. Commercial radar target simulators are expensive, while sub-6 GHz ISAC experiments often need only tens of megahertz of bandwidth within their available spectrum allocation. This makes simpler, low-cost test hardware attractive. We present a low-cost, open-source radar target simulator based on an ADALM-Pluto without hardware modification, supporting four independently configurable targets and analog bandwidths up to 56 MHz. The FPGA generates echoes with independent delays, Doppler shifts and gains, using fractional-delay filters for sub-sample adjustment. For motion-consistent echoes, delay and carrier phase are updated together to reproduce both changing range and frequency-dependent Doppler shifts. Over-the-air measurements demonstrate simultaneous echoes, sub-sample delay adjustment, and smooth target motion between sample positions. The FPGA source, firmware and on-device web interface are publicly available.

A: We study the least-cost co-expansion of power distribution networks and public charging ports to accommodate the growth of electric vehicles (EVs). Our approach, MAC+, exploits the flexibility of charging along each EV's itinerary and coordinates it across the fleet to reduce the peak violations of each feeder's hosting capacity and port capacity. This coordination is an extremely large, spatio-temporally coupled optimization problem with binary plug-in variables. We solve it by iterated price response (IPR), which repeatedly posts a two-tier tariff on feeder load and port occupancy, lets millions of EVs best-respond in parallel, and certifies the optimality gap at every iteration. We develop a custom exact dynamic-programming algorithm that solves each EV's best-response problem, a mixed-integer quadratic program, about 20 times faster than off-the-shelf solvers. The case study covers the San Francisco Bay Area at 30% EV adoption, with 1.8 million EVs on week-long itineraries and 1,303 feeder service regions, each with a utility-published hosting capacity and a port capacity set by its existing public ports. On this instance, IPR reaches a certified gap below 10% in a few hours. MAC+ saves about $15 billion of the upgrade investment that unmanaged charging would require. It also needs over 90% less investment than charging that is fully coordinated but flexible only within each session, and over 80% less than charging that is flexible along the itinerary but uncoordinated.

A: AI data centers exhibit highly stochastic, volatile power demands from intensive workloads and synchronized GPU training cycles, which can excite grid natural frequencies and threaten system stability. This paper proposes a real-time, forecasting-independent control framework utilizing a Hybrid Energy Storage System (HESS) that coordinates a Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) and a supercapacitor (SC). Employing a parameterized frequency-decoupling and active modal-damping policy, the framework mitigates critical oscillatory load components while smoothing overall power fluctuations. To bypass the heavy computational burden of online receding-horizon optimization, this work introduces an offline Bayesian Optimization (BO) approach to optimally tune real-time control parameters, minimizing a multi-objective cost function that balances grid compliance penalties and storage degradation. Numerical simulations demonstrate that the proposed method ensures grid stability and strong target envelope adherence. Specifically, it reshapes extreme 75-160 MW raw demand fluctuations to largely fit within a tight 10 MW target band, with only brief transient excursions, while attenuating the critical 20 MW oscillatory component below 1 MW to suppress resonant excitation.

A: Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) reachability provides certified backward reachable tubes (BRTs) for safety-critical robotic systems, but the level-set computation scales exponentially in the state dimension and has historically been performed offline. As autonomy stacks (ADAS/AV, humanoid robotics, and vision-language-action models) increasingly rely on black-box, probabilistic policies, a deterministic safety layer with formal guarantees is an essential complement. We present a CUDA implementation of the canonical WENO5 + TVD-RK3 + Lax-Friedrichs level-set Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs solver for 2D, 3D, and 4D dynamics that is fast enough to run inside a robot's control loop. In 64-bit floating point (FP64) it agrees with hj_reachability on eight benchmark cases, reproduces Mitchell's Air3D BRT to within 0.04% of the reference cell count, and runs 2.0-4.6x faster. On an embedded NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor it computes Air3D at 66 Hz (N=41) and the 2D drifter at 54 Hz, 3.8-8.9x faster than hj_reachability on the same device. As a multi-agent application, an in-kernel label-propagation extension recovers the K-agent capture-basin Voronoi tessellation from a single combined HJ solve, independent of fleet size; it runs at 4.0 ms per tick in a closed-loop wildfire-response simulation of six quadcopters under time-varying, non-uniform wind.

A: Heterogeneous air-ground teams can use aerial sensing to address the limited range and viewpoint of ground-vehicle sensors, but deciding when the UGV needs assistance and what information the UAV should collect remains a challenge. This paper presents a planner-conditioned air-ground assistance method that evaluates how uncertain map information affects the UGV's current MPPI rollouts. When navigation remains degraded, we score the same rollouts under resolved map hypotheses, select the map layer with the largest useful improvement, request the corresponding aerial measurement, fuse the returned information, and replan. Unlike approaches driven by fixed support roles, task structure, or uncertainty alone, our method conditions assistance on whether resolving uncertainty improves predicted ground navigation. Across 180 simulation trials on three off-road routes, the method achieves 98.9% goal attainment while reducing mean UAV flight time by 87.7% relative to continuous greedy aerial mapping. Aggregated across the routes, each second of estimated UAV flight time saves 2.94 s of UGV navigation time. Field experiments spanning approximately 2 km of UGV operation demonstrate uncertainty resolution and successful navigation recovery.

A: This paper presents a novel method for converting the divergent Gaussian intensity distribution of a millimeter-wave source into a uniform (flat-top) distribution using a single curved surface. The proposed method combines the surface profile of a collimator with that of a beam shaper. To validate the method, the profile of a single-sided (plano-convex) lens is derived and placed 52 mm in front of a conical horn antenna operating at 100 GHz. The lens transforms the Gaussian radiation of the horn, with an incident beam radius of 11.9 mm, into a uniform beam with a radius of 400 mm at a distance of 3 m. The lens surface profile is optimized using a full-wave-simulation-based procedure, and the resulting output beam is compared with that of a previously designed double-sided (concave-convex) lens. Simulation results show that, within the desired field of view, the optimized single-sided lens produces a flat-top intensity distribution with satisfactory ripple and roll-off. Finally, the sensitivity of the optimized lens to frequency variation is investigated. The proposed lens is suitable for generating uniform illumination in active stand-off millimeter-wave imaging systems.

A: The increasing penetration of converter-interfaced generation reduces system inertia, short-circuit strength, and voltage support. European grid codes, including the ENTSO-E Network Code on Requirements for Generators and the ACER Demand Connection Code, now define disturbance-based validation procedures for grid-forming (GFM) generation and converter-based demand. Commercial RMS tools, however, lack an integrated workflow aligned with these recent requirements. This paper presents an automated Python-PowerFactory compliance toolbox and an RMS test bench for a co-located system comprising a 1 MW GFM photovoltaic (PV) plant, a 0.3 MW GFM battery energy storage system (BESS), and a 1 MW converter-interfaced dynamic load at a 20 kV point of common coupling fed from a 110 kV grid. Extended virtual synchronous machine models and a DCC-oriented load model are tested in batch, with results automatically extracted and plotted for assessment. Results show compliant RMS performance for the slower, electromechanical tests, while the paper identifies which tests require complementary electromagnetic transient (EMT) verification.

A: In this paper, a novel, to our knowledge, analytical approach is introduced for the design of a single-sided plano-convex lens (PCL) capable of terahertz (THz) flat-top beam shaping in the Fresnel region. The lens profile, derived from geometrical optics principles, integrates collimating and beam-shaping functions into a single optical surface, thereby simplifying fabrication. The efficiency of the method is demonstrated by designing two PCLs that convert a divergent Gaussian beam from a monochromatic THz source (at 100 and 200 GHz) into flat-top beams with target radii of 400 and 500 mm at distances of 3 and 4 m, respectively. The resulting fields, evaluated through analytical, integral equation, and finite element techniques, are shown to be comparable to those produced by a conventional double-sided concave-convex lens. Furthermore, the sensitivity of the design to frequency and alignment variations is investigated, confirming the robustness of this single-curvature approach for integration into practical THz imaging systems.

A: Patient-specific airway modelling requires geometrically consistent lumen surfaces with identifiable boundaries and support for controlled anatomical modifications. We present CT-RespGeomLib, a deterministic framework that converts CT airway masks into two complementary representations: an editable assembly of semantically labelled pipe and junction blocks connected through canonical shared ports, and a fused lumen surface reconstructed from tapered implicit primitives with validated port-to-boundary loop correspondence. The parametric representation further enables localised modelling of airway stenosis and dilation without re-segmentation. Evaluated on 42 reference airway masks from ATM22 (15 cases) and AeroPath (27 cases), the framework produced 37 topologically accepted reconstructions, with a median port-to-loop distance of 0.123 mm across 2174 matched ports. Reconstructed and reference equivalent radii showed strong agreement ($R^2 = 0.976$), with a mean bias of -0.414 mm arising primarily from the circular, inscribed-radius representation. Controlled pathology modelling generated 40 variants across five patient-specific geometries, including 25-75% stenosis and 50% dilation at tracheal and main-bronchus locations. Prescribed radius changes were reproduced with a mean absolute ratio error of 0.0056, while the median 95th-percentile deviation outside the modified region was 0.111 mm. Downstream applicability was demonstrated through volume meshing and an OpenFOAM simulation with individually prescribed model-based resistance conditions at 62 outlets. Although additional surface preparation may be required for numerical meshing, CT-RespGeomLib provides a reproducible framework for CT-derived airway reconstruction, quantitative boundary validation and controlled geometric pathology modelling.

The parametric representation further enables localised modelling of airway stenosis and dilation without re-segmentation. Evaluated on 42 reference airway masks from ATM22 (15 cases) and AeroPath (27 cases), the framework produced 37 topologically accepted reconstructions, with a median port-to-loop distance of 0.123 mm across 2174 matched ports. Reconstructed and reference equivalent radii showed strong agreement ($R^2 = 0.976$), with a mean bias of -0.414 mm arising primarily from the circular, inscribed-radius representation. Controlled pathology modelling generated 40 variants across five patient-specific geometries, including 25-75% stenosis and 50% dilation at tracheal and main-bronchus locations. Prescribed radius changes were reproduced with a mean absolute ratio error of 0.0056, while the median 95th-percentile deviation outside the modified region was 0.111 mm. Downstream applicability was demonstrated through volume meshing and an OpenFOAM simulation with individually prescribed model-based resistance conditions at 62 outlets. Although additional surface preparation may be required for numerical meshing, CT-RespGeomLib provides a reproducible framework for CT-derived airway reconstruction, quantitative boundary validation and controlled geometric pathology modelling.

A: LiDAR-based localization and mapping systems produce registered point clouds that serve as geometric measurements for downstream estimation and navigation. Registration errors introduce duplicated surfaces and structural deformation into these measurements. In the absence of an independent reference, online assessment relies on geometry accumulated from earlier measurements. Such assessment requires tolerance to sampling variation and an accumulation process in which observations enter the history only after evaluation. We therefore formulate a recursive Bayesian comparison that couples geometric assessment with history maintenance. A Normal-Inverse-Wishart model represents historical voxel geometry and its uncertainty, while a weak isotropic reference adapts to current sampling. Comparing the marginal predictive support of the same current points under both models yields Normalized Drift Evidence (NDE). Assessment precedes assimilation: positive NDE triggers an alarm and preserves the preceding historical state; otherwise, the current observations update the history. Across 14 real-world sequences totaling approximately 73 min from four platform types, alarms identified all nine corrupted sequences and were absent from all five consistent sequences. In four representative scenarios with event references, first alarms occurred within 0.9 s of the reference times, with no preceding alarms. Cross-backend evaluation demonstrates consistent responses to reconstructed geometry. Ablation and controlled perturbation results establish the roles of uncertainty modeling, recursive history, displacement, and geometric support. Mean processing time is 4.2--6.1 ms per update at 1 Hz. In ten UAV trials, alarms initiated odometry isolation, landing, relocalization, and mission continuation.

A: Oscillatory power components in AI data-center demand can produce large frequency deviations when they coincide with vulnerable grid modes. Mode-aware hybrid energy storage systems (HESSs) can selectively suppress these components, but their effectiveness degrades when the grid mode changes while the control target remains fixed. This paper proposes a closed-loop grid-mode-adaptive HESS control framework that integrates measurement-based modal identification with mode-selective control. A sliding-window N4SID estimator identifies the local grid dynamics from grid-side power and frequency measurements, and the resulting natural-frequency estimate is used to retune the modal suppression branch assigned to the supercapacitor. The framework is evaluated under a grid-mode shift from 0.50 to 1.35Hz while maintaining equal physical damping and approximately equal load excitation at both frequencies. Compared with the fixed-target controller, the adaptive method reduces the post-change grid-side modal power component from 8.78 to 2.02MW, corresponding to a 76.94% reduction, and substantially lowers the resulting frequency deviation.

A: Maze navigation requires localization from sparse, repetitive geometry, planning through narrow corridors, and control that stays safe when the estimate or the map is wrong. We present Maze Runner, an open autonomy stack in C++ and ROS 2 that addresses these needs end to end on a simulated Husarion ROSbot XL with a 2D LiDAR in Gazebo. Perception extracts wall lines from each scan with RANSAC and total least squares, with per-line uncertainty. The same line front end feeds two estimators: an Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) that localizes against a line map built from the maze mesh, and an EKF SLAM variant that builds the line map online. Planning runs online on an inflated occupancy grid with A* plus line-of-sight shortcutting, or with a forward-only Hybrid A*. A nonlinear Model Predictive Controller (NMPC) tracks the plan while discrete-time Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) on world-frame LiDAR points keep the robot clear of walls and unmapped obstacles. The algorithms live in a ROS-free, unit-tested core library, and the whole stack builds and runs from a single reproducible environment. In simulation, the robot drives a 135 m route through the maze with 1.0 cm localization RMSE against the known map and 24 cm in SLAM mode, the planner returns a path in 6 ms, and the NMPC solves in 11.7 ms on average, never exceeding its 80 ms budget.

A: Many rehabilitation robots execute prescribed motions using reactive tracking controllers that do not explicitly incorporate the user's instantaneous human-ground interaction. This paper presents Ground Reaction Force-Aware Model Predictive Control (GRF-MPC), a framework for upright physical assistance. By integrating live GRF and center of pressure (CoP) measurements directly into a human centroidal dynamics model, GRF-MPC formulates a real-time quadratic program (QP) that optimizes assistive forces and moments over a receding horizon. We deployed GRF-MPC on the Robotic Upright Stand Trainer (RobUST) in an underactuated 4-cable configuration and evaluated it against a fully actuated 8-cable Cartesian impedance baseline in nearly 300 trials across six healthy participants. Across tasks spanning impulsive perturbations, lunge trajectories, and voluntary limits of stability, GRF-MPC reduced peak planar center-of-mass (CoM) error by 19.6% during perturbations, lowered trajectory tracking error by 24.1%, required 28.7% less net mechanical work, and permitted a 45.9% greater normalized voluntary excursion area. The underlying QP solves in under 1 ms, comfortably enabling 100 Hz replanning and demonstrating that incorporating live human-ground interaction into predictive control yields stronger, more transparent physical assistance with half the actuators.

A: Autonomous racing provides a demanding testbed for collision avoidance under tight geometric and computational constraints. Building on a recent conference contribution and a master's dissertation, LACART combines lookahead-based control barrier functions (CBFs), a relaxed control Lyapunov function (CLF), and quadratic programming (QP) to modify nominal vehicle commands for obstacle avoidance and reference tracking. The method handles circular obstacles and track boundaries in a common optimisation layer. Comparative simulation results against Huang \emph{et al.} \cite{r9} show similar full-track paths and lower median computation times: 0.31 versus 0.33 ms per step and 0.023 versus 0.025 ms per QP solve. The dissertation further demonstrates a 1:43-scale vehicle with camera-based estimation and wireless actuation at a reported 25 Hz control rate. We identify the conditions linking lookahead-point clearance to body clearance, illustrate hardware limitations, and propose a recorded demonstration of safety intervention and recovery. The contribution targets ground-robot collision avoidance and real-time safety monitoring.

A: Monitoring the relative radiometric stability of the European Space Agency's BIOMASS P-band synthetic aperture radar (SAR) requires separating instrumental and processing effects from temporal changes in the scene backscatter. This study investigates the use of permanent scatterers (PSs) as opportunistic references for estimating residual radiometric gains without dedicated calibration targets. The PS-based calibration (PSCal) framework combines amplitude-based scatterer selection with iterative maximum-likelihood gain estimation. Simulations assess detection and estimation performance under the limited number of acquisitions available in BIOMASS stacks, highlighting the importance of stringent selection thresholds and the dependence of estimation accuracy on scatterer abundance and signal-to-noise ratio. The approach is applied to datasets over Nairobi, Kenya, and Cordoba, Argentina. Over Nairobi, PSCal identifies an approximately 1 dB radiometric anomaly subsequently traced to a defect in radio-frequency interference mitigation, while the remaining acquisitions exhibit estimated gain variations generally within 0.1 dB. Over Cordoba, twelve acquisitions spanning two mission phases separated by approximately eight months yield residual gain variations on the order of 0.1 dB despite pronounced changes in the scene backscatter and acquisition geometry. Results were observed to be consistent with measurements from the BIOMASS Calibration Transponder (BCT) installed in New Norcia (Australia). These results demonstrate the potential of carefully selected P-band PSs to complement dedicated calibration infrastructure for relative radiometric monitoring and the detection of processing anomalies.

A: Deep-learning unrolled networks are the leading approach to accelerated MRI reconstruction. State-of-the-art models such as PromptMR+ learn a distinct block for every cascade, so their size grows with the number of cascades. Sharing one block across iterations avoids adding parameters, but earlier shared-weight models typically used a tiny block and produced worse images than models with distinct weights. Therefore, it remained unclear whether weight sharing itself or the choice of block was the problem. Recent advances in looped transformers, which reuse the same block across layers, show that they can match or outperform their distinct-weight counterparts on several tasks. Motivated by this, we propose LoopMR, which reuses a single Restormer block at every iteration as its core. Besides the current image estimate, the block receives data-consistency inputs and latent images. On four datasets covering the brain (CC359), knee (fastMRI), heart (CMRxRecon2023) and carotid (in-house), LoopMR significantly outperforms E2E-VarNet, PromptMR and PromptMR+ in PSNR and SSIM at every acceleration factor (p < 0.01), with about 1/9 of PromptMR+'s parameters (10.3M versus 92.9M). It also keeps its lead at unseen acceleration factors and on an unseen dataset. With our transformer block, the shared model matches or outperforms its distinct-weight counterpart at 6, 12 and 24 iterations. At a fixed number of iterations, shared transformer blocks match or outperform their distinct-weight versions, while shared CNN blocks perform worse. These results suggest that looping one well-chosen block can outperform stacking distinct cascades in MRI reconstruction, with a fraction of the parameters.

A: Objectives: High-Speed Videoendoscopy glottal area waveforms conflate lateral fold excursion with longitudinal opening, precluding direct estimation of velocity, acceleration, and left-right asymmetry. Displacement waveforms preserve these quantities but are susceptible to spatial quantization and temporal sampling errors. We characterize these errors, evaluate reduction via Kalman smoothing and temporal interpolation, and determine optimal frame rate bounds relative to pixel excursion, speed quotient (SQ), and open quotient (OQ). Methods: Sampling theory was used to derive analytical frame-rate bounds required for kinematic feature fidelity. Kalman smoothing was compared with FFT-based denoising, paired with sinc or spline interpolation. Interpolation was evaluated on 4000 fps recordings (N=55) downsampled and reconstructed. A 16000 fps dataset (N=12) served as reference for noise reduction across 2000-8000 fps downsampled waveforms evaluated on peak displacement, velocity, OQ, and SQ. Results: Sinc interpolation yielded lower median mean absolute error than spline (0.29 vs 0.52 pixels), with 85% of recordings (47/55) versus 45% (25/55) below 0.5 pixels. For kinematic feature estimation (N=12), Kalman-sinc outperformed FFT-sinc in 75% of feature-by-frame-rate pairings. Conclusion: Computing kinematic features without artifacts requires joint consideration of temporal and spatial resolution. Kalman-sinc preprocessing at 8000 fps is recommended for velocity and SQ measures. Peak lateral displacement can be measured at 2000 fps, while OQ requires 4000 fps for typical spatial resolutions (9-14 pixels maximum excursion). Pixel excursion should be reported alongside kinematic measures to contextualize data reliability.

A: Single-image HDR reconstruction requires inferring missing detail while preserving the visible content of an LDR image. Differences in sensor dynamic range and exposure cause LDR images to lose varying amounts of information in shadows and highlights. We present ExpandDiff, a conditional diffusion pipeline that jointly reconstructs clipped shadows and highlights. To account for this variation, we introduce Dynamic Clipping Synthesis (DCS), which randomly samples shadow and highlight clipping percentiles when constructing training inputs from HDR targets. A pixel-space diffusion model guided by spatially-adaptive normalization then predicts perceptually encoded HDR through a bounded output head, reconstructing both clipping directions in one sampling trajectory. On the SI-HDR benchmark, ExpandDiff variants improve HDR reconstruction accuracy by 3.43 dB in PU21-PSNR over the strongest evaluated competing method, and by 7.34 dB under two-sided clipping. The code and supplementary material are available at https://memreandiran.github.io/expanddiff/.
