A: The increasing penetration of converter-interfaced generation reduces system inertia, short-circuit strength, and voltage support. European grid codes, including the ENTSO-E Network Code on Requirements for Generators and the ACER Demand Connection Code, now define disturbance-based validation procedures for grid-forming (GFM) generation and converter-based demand. Commercial RMS tools, however, lack an integrated workflow aligned with these recent requirements. This paper presents an automated Python-PowerFactory compliance toolbox and an RMS test bench for a co-located system comprising a 1 MW GFM photovoltaic (PV) plant, a 0.3 MW GFM battery energy storage system (BESS), and a 1 MW converter-interfaced dynamic load at a 20 kV point of common coupling fed from a 110 kV grid. Extended virtual synchronous machine models and a DCC-oriented load model are tested in batch, with results automatically extracted and plotted for assessment. Results show compliant RMS performance for the slower, electromechanical tests, while the paper identifies which tests require complementary electromagnetic transient (EMT) verification.
I: In systems and control, the rise of converter-based generation has brought about challenges like lowered system inertia, short-circuit power, and voltage support. New grid codes from ENTSO-E and ACER now outline tests for grid-forming units and converter-connected loads. But current commercial RMS tools don't fully meet these requirements with an automated Python-PowerFactory tool for compliance and an RMS test setup we've got, featuring a 1 MW GFM PV plant, a 0.3 MW GFM BESS, and a 1 MW dynamic load on a 20 kV bus fed by a 110 kV grid. We used extended virtual synchronous machines and a DCC model for testing in batch, with the findings automatically charted. This shows that RMS works well for tests like electromechanical ones, but we see a need for EMT checks for some tests. A: In this paper, a novel, to our knowledge, analytical approach is introduced for the design of a single-sided plano-convex lens (PCL) capable of terahertz (THz) flat-top beam shaping in the Fresnel region. The lens profile, derived from geometrical optics principles, integrates collimating and beam-shaping functions into a single optical surface, thereby simplifying fabrication. The efficiency of the method is demonstrated by designing two PCLs that convert a divergent Gaussian beam from a monochromatic THz source (at 100 and 200 GHz) into flat-top beams with target radii of 400 and 500 mm at distances of 3 and 4 m, respectively. The resulting fields, evaluated through analytical, integral equation, and finite element techniques, are shown to be comparable to those produced by a conventional double-sided concave-convex lens. Furthermore, the sensitivity of the design to frequency and alignment variations is investigated, confirming the robustness of this single-curvature approach for integration into practical THz imaging systems.
I: In our study, we introduce a new analytical method for designing single-sided plano-convex lenses (PCLs) for shaping terahertz (THz) flat-top beams. Based on geometrical optics, our lens design combines collimation and beam shaping onto one surface, making it easier to produce. We successfully showed how two of these lenses can transform a Gaussian beam from a THz source (100 GHz and 200 GHz) into flat-top beams of 400 mm and 500 mm radius at 3 m and 4 m, respectively. We compared the results using analytical, integral equation, and finite element methods, and found they're similar to what you'd get with traditional double-sided concave-convex lenses. Additionally, we looked into how changes in frequency and alignment affect the design, proving this single-curvature method's reliability for THz imaging systems.

A: Patient-specific airway modelling requires geometrically consistent lumen surfaces with identifiable boundaries and support for controlled anatomical modifications. We present CT-RespGeomLib, a deterministic framework that converts CT airway masks into two complementary representations: an editable assembly of semantically labelled pipe and junction blocks connected through canonical shared ports, and a fused lumen surface reconstructed from tapered implicit primitives with validated port-to-boundary loop correspondence. The parametric representation further enables localised modelling of airway stenosis and dilation without re-segmentation. Evaluated on 42 reference airway masks from ATM22 (15 cases) and AeroPath (27 cases), the framework produced 37 topologically accepted reconstructions, with a median port-to-loop distance of 0.123 mm across 2174 matched ports. Reconstructed and reference equivalent radii showed strong agreement ($R^2 = 0.976$), with a mean bias of -0.414 mm arising primarily from the circular, inscribed-radius representation. Controlled pathology modelling generated 40 variants across five patient-specific geometries, including 25-75% stenosis and 50% dilation at tracheal and main-bronchus locations. Prescribed radius changes were reproduced with a mean absolute ratio error of 0.0056, while the median 95th-percentile deviation outside the modified region was 0.111 mm. Downstream applicability was demonstrated through volume meshing and an OpenFOAM simulation with individually prescribed model-based resistance conditions at 62 outlets. Although additional surface preparation may be required for numerical meshing, CT-RespGeomLib provides a reproducible framework for CT-derived airway reconstruction, quantitative boundary validation and controlled geometric pathology modelling.
I: We've developed CT-RespGeomLib, a framework that takes CT airway masks and turns them into two parts: a pieceable collection of pipe and junction blocks with standard ports, and a unified lumen surface built from shrinking shapes, ensuring ports and boundaries line up well. On 42 airway masks, including 15 from ATM22 and 27 from AeroPath, we got 37 reconstructions that the system accepted, with an average port-to-loop gap of just 0.123 mm for 2174 ports. The match-up between our reconstructed surfaces and the real ones showed a strong fit ($R^2 = 0.976$), though there's a slight average bias of -0.414 mm mainly due to the inner circular shape. We made changes to simulate pathologies like 25-75% airway narrowing or 50% expansion in the trachea and main bronchus for five individuals, and our results hold up with a mean error of 0.0056 and a median 95th-percentile variation of 0.111 mm. We tried this in volume meshing and an OpenFOAM simulation for 62 outputs, indicating how this method can be used for airway modeling with CT data. Still, we might need to prepare the surface a bit more for numerical meshing, but overall, our CT-RespGeomLib method offers a repeatable way to turn CTs into airway models, check the accuracy of boundaries, and model airway changes like blockages or expansions.

A: Patient-specific airway modelling requires geometrically consistent lumen surfaces with identifiable boundaries and support for controlled anatomical modifications. We present CT-RespGeomLib, a deterministic framework that converts CT airway masks into two complementary representations: an editable assembly of semantically labelled pipe and junction blocks connected through canonical shared ports, and a fused lumen surface reconstructed from tapered implicit primitives with validated port-to-boundary loop correspondence. The parametric representation further enables localised modelling of airway stenosis and dilation without re-segmentation. Evaluated on 42 reference airway masks from ATM22 (15 cases) and AeroPath (27 cases), the framework produced 37 topologically accepted reconstructions, with a median port-to-loop distance of 0.123 mm across 2174 matched ports. Reconstructed and reference equivalent radii showed strong agreement ($R^2 = 0.976$), with a mean bias of -0.414 mm arising primarily from the circular, inscribed-radius representation. Controlled pathology modelling generated 40 variants across five patient-specific geometries, including 25-75% stenosis and 50% dilation at tracheal and main-bronchus locations. Prescribed radius changes were reproduced with a mean absolute ratio error of 0.0056, while the median 95th-percentile deviation outside the modified region was 0.111 mm. Downstream applicability was demonstrated through volume meshing and an OpenFOAM simulation with individually prescribed model-based resistance conditions at 62 outlets. Although additional surface preparation may be required for numerical meshing, CT-RespGeomLib provides a reproducible framework for CT-derived airway reconstruction, quantitative boundary validation and controlled geometric pathology modelling.

A: Oscillatory power components in AI data-center demand can produce large frequency deviations when they coincide with vulnerable grid modes. Mode-aware hybrid energy storage systems (HESSs) can selectively suppress these components, but their effectiveness degrades when the grid mode changes while the control target remains fixed. This paper proposes a closed-loop grid-mode-adaptive HESS control framework that integrates measurement-based modal identification with mode-selective control. A sliding-window N4SID estimator identifies the local grid dynamics from grid-side power and frequency measurements, and the resulting natural-frequency estimate is used to retune the modal suppression branch assigned to the supercapacitor. The framework is evaluated under a grid-mode shift from 0.50 to 1.35Hz while maintaining equal physical damping and approximately equal load excitation at both frequencies. Compared with the fixed-target controller, the adaptive method reduces the post-change grid-side modal power component from 8.78 to 2.02MW, corresponding to a 76.94% reduction, and substantially lowers the resulting frequency deviation.

We've found that mode-aware hybrid energy storage systems (HESSs) can dial down these swings, but they don't work as well when the grid's weak spot shifts and the control goal doesn't. So, we're working on a closed-loop control setup that adapts to the grid's changing modes, using measurements to figure out the grid's behavior and tweaking the control for the supercapacitor accordingly. We tested this approach as the grid's weak spot moved from 0.50 to 1.35Hz, with the same level of damping and roughly the same load. This adaptive strategy slashed the grid-side modal power component from 8.78MW down to 2.02MW, which is a massive 76.94% drop, and really cut down on frequency swings.

A: Maze navigation requires localization from sparse, repetitive geometry, planning through narrow corridors, and control that stays safe when the estimate or the map is wrong. We present Maze Runner, an open autonomy stack in C++ and ROS 2 that addresses these needs end to end on a simulated Husarion ROSbot XL with a 2D LiDAR in Gazebo. Perception extracts wall lines from each scan with RANSAC and total least squares, with per-line uncertainty. The same line front end feeds two estimators: an Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) that localizes against a line map built from the maze mesh, and an EKF SLAM variant that builds the line map online. Planning runs online on an inflated occupancy grid with A* plus line-of-sight shortcutting, or with a forward-only Hybrid A*. A nonlinear Model Predictive Controller (NMPC) tracks the plan while discrete-time Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) on world-frame LiDAR points keep the robot clear of walls and unmapped obstacles. The algorithms live in a ROS-free, unit-tested core library, and the whole stack builds and runs from a single reproducible environment. In simulation, the robot drives a 135 m route through the maze with 1.0 cm localization RMSE against the known map and 24 cm in SLAM mode, the planner returns a path in 6 ms, and the NMPC solves in 11.7 ms on average, never exceeding its 80 ms budget.

This information then goes to two main estimators: an Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) that navigates using a line map derived from the maze geometry, and another EKF variant that's a SLAM approach, actively constructing the line map as we go. Our codebase consists of a standalone, fully unit-tested library, and we've got everything from core to complete stack operating from a singular, reproducible setup. Testing in simulation, our Husarion ROSbot XL managed to complete a 135-meter maze course with a localization error of just 1.0 cm on a predefined map and 24 cm in SLAM mode, while our planner calculates the best route in a slick 6 ms, and our NMPC keeps its average solution time at 11.7 ms, all within the 80 ms budget limit.

A: Many rehabilitation robots execute prescribed motions using reactive tracking controllers that do not explicitly incorporate the user's instantaneous human-ground interaction. This paper presents Ground Reaction Force-Aware Model Predictive Control (GRF-MPC), a framework for upright physical assistance. By integrating live GRF and center of pressure (CoP) measurements directly into a human centroidal dynamics model, GRF-MPC formulates a real-time quadratic program (QP) that optimizes assistive forces and moments over a receding horizon. We deployed GRF-MPC on the Robotic Upright Stand Trainer (RobUST) in an underactuated 4-cable configuration and evaluated it against a fully actuated 8-cable Cartesian impedance baseline in nearly 300 trials across six healthy participants. Across tasks spanning impulsive perturbations, lunge trajectories, and voluntary limits of stability, GRF-MPC reduced peak planar center-of-mass (CoM) error by 19.6% during perturbations, lowered trajectory tracking error by 24.1%, required 28.7% less net mechanical work, and permitted a 45.9% greater normalized voluntary excursion area. The underlying QP solves in under 1 ms, comfortably enabling 100 Hz replanning and demonstrating that incorporating live human-ground interaction into predictive control yields stronger, more transparent physical assistance with half the actuators.

A: Autonomous racing provides a demanding testbed for collision avoidance under tight geometric and computational constraints. Building on a recent conference contribution and a master's dissertation, LACART combines lookahead-based control barrier functions (CBFs), a relaxed control Lyapunov function (CLF), and quadratic programming (QP) to modify nominal vehicle commands for obstacle avoidance and reference tracking. The method handles circular obstacles and track boundaries in a common optimisation layer. Comparative simulation results against Huang \emph{et al.} \cite{r9} show similar full-track paths and lower median computation times: 0.31 versus 0.33 ms per step and 0.023 versus 0.025 ms per QP solve. The dissertation further demonstrates a 1:43-scale vehicle with camera-based estimation and wireless actuation at a reported 25 Hz control rate. We identify the conditions linking lookahead-point clearance to body clearance, illustrate hardware limitations, and propose a recorded demonstration of safety intervention and recovery. The contribution targets ground-robot collision avoidance and real-time safety monitoring.

A: Monitoring the relative radiometric stability of the European Space Agency's BIOMASS P-band synthetic aperture radar (SAR) requires separating instrumental and processing effects from temporal changes in the scene backscatter. This study investigates the use of permanent scatterers (PSs) as opportunistic references for estimating residual radiometric gains without dedicated calibration targets. The PS-based calibration (PSCal) framework combines amplitude-based scatterer selection with iterative maximum-likelihood gain estimation. Simulations assess detection and estimation performance under the limited number of acquisitions available in BIOMASS stacks, highlighting the importance of stringent selection thresholds and the dependence of estimation accuracy on scatterer abundance and signal-to-noise ratio. The approach is applied to datasets over Nairobi, Kenya, and Cordoba, Argentina. Over Nairobi, PSCal identifies an approximately 1 dB radiometric anomaly subsequently traced to a defect in radio-frequency interference mitigation, while the remaining acquisitions exhibit estimated gain variations generally within 0.1 dB. Over Cordoba, twelve acquisitions spanning two mission phases separated by approximately eight months yield residual gain variations on the order of 0.1 dB despite pronounced changes in the scene backscatter and acquisition geometry. Results were observed to be consistent with measurements from the BIOMASS Calibration Transponder (BCT) installed in New Norcia (Australia). These results demonstrate the potential of carefully selected P-band PSs to complement dedicated calibration infrastructure for relative radiometric monitoring and the detection of processing anomalies.
I: In our work, we look into how to check the radiometric stability of the European Space Agency's (ESA's) BIOMASS P-band SAR, by separating out stuff from the scene changes using permanent scatterers (PSs). We use a PSCal framework for this, which picks PSs based on their scatterer levels and refines gain estimations through an iterative process. By running simulations with the limited data we got from the BIOMASS stacks, we see how crucial it is to be strict about our PS selection and how the accuracy depends on the number of PSs and how clear they are. We put this method to test over Nairobi and Cordoba, finding that in Nairobi, we found about a 1 dB anomaly linked to some interference issue, while the other images were mostly stable with less than 0.1 dB variation. Over Cordoba, we saw small gain changes, still less than 0.1 dB, even with big changes in the scene and the way the images were taken. The findings matched up with the BIOMASS Calibration Transponder (BCT) data from New Norcia. Our results suggest that with good PS choices, we can use them to support calibration efforts and catch processing errors. (Word count: 250)

I: We dove into the world of image and video processing for the European Space Agency's BIOMASS P-band SAR, where keeping things steady's key. I: Alright, so here's a rough draft on this image and video processing thing. We're looking at how we can keep track of the BIOMASS P-band SAR's radiometric stability, you know? The key is figuring out those pesky instrumental and processing quirks from the actual scene changes. A: Pretrained Earth observation models may reduce the effort needed to map surface water, but their value depends on the alternative against which they are compared. We evaluated Prithvi-EO-2.0-Tiny using the 446 hand-labeled Sentinel-2 chips from 11 flood events in Sen1Floods11. A fine-tuned model, a frozen-encoder model, and an identical randomly initialized architecture were compared with a similarly sized U-Net, a larger Prithvi model, and spectral-index thresholds. Experiments varied the number of training chips, excluded events from model fitting, and measured computational cost and prediction reliability. With 252 training chips, U-Net achieved a water intersection-over-union (IoU) of 0.856 on the official test set, compared with 0.833 for fine-tuned Prithvi-Tiny. Pretraining improved the tiny transformer over random initialization by a reported 0.046 IoU with 25 training chips and 0.023 with 252 chips, but did not reverse the U-Net ranking. Across 11 event-exclusion evaluations, mean IoU was 0.768 for fine-tuned Prithvi-Tiny and 0.777 for U-Net; the paired interval included zero. Fine-tuned Prithvi-Tiny processed a 512x512-pixel chip in 16.1 ms on a GPU and 258 ms on a laptop CPU, compared with 30.6 and 665 ms for U-Net. Errors were concentrated near water boundaries, and high predictive entropy identified many, but not all, erroneous pixels. These results support a specific role for compact pretrained models: lower measured computational demand with competitive accuracy, rather than consistent superiority. Event-dependent performance, shared hyperparameter selection, and the distinction between observed water and newly inundated land delimit the conclusions.

We also compared it to a U-Net model, a larger Prithvi model, and spectral-index thresholds. We tried different training chip quantities, excluded some events during training, and checked how much computational power was needed and how reliable the predictions were. We found out that using 252 training chips, U-Net had better water IoU (0.856) than fine-tuned Prithvi-Tiny (0.833). Pretraining seemed to help the tiny transformer a bit (0.046 IoU with 25 chips and 0.023 with 252 chips), but it didn't change the U-Net's lead. We noticed that mistakes were mostly near water edges, and we saw high entropy in some wrong predictions. This suggests that small pretrained models can be good for lower computational costs and fairly accurate results, rather than always being the best choice. We have to consider event-specific performance, consistent parameter choices, and clear water vs. inundated land distinctions.

A: LOL-v1 and LOLv2-Real are the standard benchmarks for supervised low-light image enhancement, and several leading methods ship hand-set test-time adjustments with their evaluation scripts. We audit both benchmarks with 18 public checkpoints of eight methods under one metric implementation that reproduces every published number to within 0.09 dB, and find that their test labels differ from their training labels. (i) The 15 LOL-v1 test labels are rendered differently: the same captures appear in LOLv2 with labels of identical luminance but 1.48x lower saturation, and LOL-v1's own training labels match the LOLv2 rendering; we confirm this on the official release. (ii) The LOLv2-Real test set is the contiguous block of images 690-789, whose labels are 14% darker than the training labels (Cliff's delta = -0.45, p < 1e-12) with no comparable shift in the input statistics we examined; methods trained without any labels score up to 5.5 dB higher on test than on train. (iii) All 15 LOL-v1 test inputs reappear in LOLv2-Real, 12 in its training set. The released test-time settings are consistent with compensating for these shifts. Separating what can be calibrated on training data from what only test-set tuning finds, the test-only residual has median 0.00 dB on LOLv2-Syn, which has no shift, but 0.37 dB on LOL-v1 and 0.92 dB on LOLv2-Real (up to 3.9 dB). Under the shift, test-set checkpoint selection inflates a from-scratch model by 0.9-2.0 dB, and removing the released settings changes which method ranks first. We give concrete reporting recommendations.
I: Hey, we checked out these image enhancement benchmarks LOL-v1 and LOLv2-Real, and found some interesting stuff. First off, we noticed that the 15 LOL-v1 tests look a bit different than their training data. The same images show up in LOLv2 with labels that are more subdued, specifically 1.48x lower in saturation, but the training labels for LOL-v1 actually match up with this new rendering. It's confirmed in the official releases. Then, we took a look at the LOLv2-Real set, which is all the images between 690 and 789. Turns out, their labels are about 14% darker compared to the training data (Cliff's delta is -0.45, and the p-value is less than 0.001). We didn't see any similar changes in the input stats we looked at. Plus, if you train without any labels, you can get up to 5.5 dB higher scores on the test than on training. Also, out of 15 LOL-v1 tests, 12 of them are also in the LOLv2-Real training set. It seems like the test-time settings they've released are doing their job to balance out these differences. We also found that the median difference is pretty low (0.00 dB) for the LOLv2-Syn set, which has no shift, but it's 0.37 dB for LOL-v1 and 0.92 dB for LOLv2-Real (up to 3.9 dB). This shows that the test-only adjustments can boost a brand new model by 0.9 to 2.0 dB. And if we take out the official settings, it changes the rankings of which method performs best. To wrap it up, we've come up with some solid guidelines for reporting based on what we've learned.

A: Deep-learning unrolled networks are the leading approach to accelerated MRI reconstruction. State-of-the-art models such as PromptMR+ learn a distinct block for every cascade, so their size grows with the number of cascades. Sharing one block across iterations avoids adding parameters, but earlier shared-weight models typically used a tiny block and produced worse images than models with distinct weights. Therefore, it remained unclear whether weight sharing itself or the choice of block was the problem. Recent advances in looped transformers, which reuse the same block across layers, show that they can match or outperform their distinct-weight counterparts on several tasks. Motivated by this, we propose LoopMR, which reuses a single Restormer block at every iteration as its core. Besides the current image estimate, the block receives data-consistency inputs and latent images. On four datasets covering the brain (CC359), knee (fastMRI), heart (CMRxRecon2023) and carotid (in-house), LoopMR significantly outperforms E2E-VarNet, PromptMR and PromptMR+ in PSNR and SSIM at every acceleration factor (p < 0.01), with about 1/9 of PromptMR+'s parameters (10.3M versus 92.9M). It also keeps its lead at unseen acceleration factors and on an unseen dataset. With our transformer block, the shared model matches or outperforms its distinct-weight counterpart at 6, 12 and 24 iterations. At a fixed number of iterations, shared transformer blocks match or outperform their distinct-weight versions, while shared CNN blocks perform worse. These results suggest that looping one well-chosen block can outperform stacking distinct cascades in MRI reconstruction, with a fraction of the parameters.

A: Image-guided surgery (IGS) depends on accurate tracking of surgical instruments to provide real-time navigation relative to anatomical structures. Commercial stereo infrared trackers are accurate but prone to occlusion and cost-prohibitive for many settings. This work presents LARK, a multi-camera optical tracking system using commodity RGB hardware and multi-view redundancy and fusion. We develop and evaluate two complete tracking methods: multi-view monocular pose fusion and multi-view triangulation. Both methods are assessed under varying occlusion levels using a precision-machined grid and an anatomical head phantom, and compared against a gold-standard stereo infrared system. With five cameras and adaptive Kalman filtering, LARK achieves median target registration errors of 0.64 mm for point localization with triangulation and 0.73 mm for trajectory tracking with pose fusion on the machined grid. Camera-subset experiments show graceful degradation in adaptive pose-fusion accuracy as fewer views remain available. With tracking hardware costing under $1,000 USD, LARK provides a low-cost platform for image-guided surgery research. Hardware designs and software are publicly available at https://nist.mni.mcgill.ca/software/ , and datasets at https://nist.mni.mcgill.ca/data/ .

We've put together LARK, a system that uses regular RGB cameras and relies on multiple perspectives to figure out where things are. We're checking out two tracking ways: combining views for better pose estimation and using multiple angles for triangulation. We're testing these methods on a precise grid and a head model to match up against traditional infrared trackers. With five cameras and smart filtering, we've hit a median error of 0.64 mm for pinpointing spots and 0.73 mm for tracing paths, which is pretty cool. We're seeing that when we use fewer camera views, the tracking gets a bit rougher. The good news is LARK is super affordable, costing less than $1,000 USD, making it a great option for research. We've also put together everything needed to build and test it, which we've shared online for anyone interested.

Displacement waveforms preserve these quantities but are susceptible to spatial quantization and temporal sampling errors. Methods: Sampling theory was used to derive analytical frame-rate bounds required for kinematic feature fidelity. Kalman smoothing was compared with FFT-based denoising, paired with sinc or spline interpolation. Interpolation was evaluated on 4000 fps recordings (N=55) downsampled and reconstructed. A 16000 fps dataset (N=12) served as reference for noise reduction across 2000-8000 fps downsampled waveforms evaluated on peak displacement, velocity, OQ, and SQ. Results: Sinc interpolation yielded lower median mean absolute error than spline (0.29 vs 0.52 pixels), with 85% of recordings (47/55) versus 45% (25/55) below 0.5 pixels. For kinematic feature estimation (N=12), Kalman-sinc outperformed FFT-sinc in 75% of feature-by-frame-rate pairings. Conclusion: Computing kinematic features without artifacts requires joint consideration of temporal and spatial resolution. Kalman-sinc preprocessing at 8000 fps is recommended for velocity and SQ measures. Peak lateral displacement can be measured at 2000 fps, while OQ requires 4000 fps for typical spatial resolutions (9-14 pixels maximum excursion). Pixel excursion should be reported alongside kinematic measures to contextualize data reliability.

A: Single-image HDR reconstruction requires inferring missing detail while preserving the visible content of an LDR image. Differences in sensor dynamic range and exposure cause LDR images to lose varying amounts of information in shadows and highlights. We present ExpandDiff, a conditional diffusion pipeline that jointly reconstructs clipped shadows and highlights. To account for this variation, we introduce Dynamic Clipping Synthesis (DCS), which randomly samples shadow and highlight clipping percentiles when constructing training inputs from HDR targets. A pixel-space diffusion model guided by spatially-adaptive normalization then predicts perceptually encoded HDR through a bounded output head, reconstructing both clipping directions in one sampling trajectory. On the SI-HDR benchmark, ExpandDiff variants improve HDR reconstruction accuracy by 3.43 dB in PU21-PSNR over the strongest evaluated competing method, and by 7.34 dB under two-sided clipping. The code and supplementary material are available at https://memreandiran.github.io/expanddiff/.

There's a problem with LDR images, where they often miss crucial info in dark or bright spots due to sensor dynamic range and exposure issues. Our study introduces ExpandDiff, a conditional diffusion technique that's jointly working on improving clipped shadows and highlights. We've put together Dynamic Clipping Synthesis (DCS) that decides different shadow and highlight clipping percentiles for training data based on HDR targets. This is then guided by a pixel-space diffusion model that uses spatially-adaptive normalization, which helps it predict and encode HDR in a way that's both perceptually sound and bounded. Our ExpandDiff method outperforms others in the SI-HDR benchmark, seeing a 3.43 dB increase in PU21-PSNR over top competitors, and a massive 7.34 dB improvement with two-sided clipping. A: Single-image HDR reconstruction requires inferring missing detail while preserving the visible content of an LDR image. Differences in sensor dynamic range and exposure cause LDR images to lose varying amounts of information in shadows and highlights. We present ExpandDiff, a conditional diffusion pipeline that jointly reconstructs clipped shadows and highlights. To account for this variation, we introduce Dynamic Clipping Synthesis (DCS), which randomly samples shadow and highlight clipping percentiles when constructing training inputs from HDR targets. A pixel-space diffusion model guided by spatially-adaptive normalization then predicts perceptually encoded HDR through a bounded output head, reconstructing both clipping directions in one sampling trajectory. On the SI-HDR benchmark, ExpandDiff variants improve HDR reconstruction accuracy by 3.43 dB in PU21-PSNR over the strongest evaluated competing method, and by 7.34 dB under two-sided clipping. The code and supplementary material are available at https://memreandiran.github.io/expanddiff/.

A: Super-resolution networks are trained for one magnification factor, so several output resolutions require several models. We propose PMS-SR, a progressive single-input multiple-output network that produces x2, x4, and x8 results in one forward pass, with a Transformer backbone on the low-resolution grid. In Stage 1, each scale is predicted as a residual over the detached bicubic upsampling of the previous scale's prediction. With Dirac and zero initialization, training starts exactly from the bicubic cascade, and each head adds only the band the previous scale lacks. In Stage 2, inter-scale mutual refinement couples the scales in both directions through space-to-depth feedback, deformable alignment, and per-pixel fusion, so x8 features refine the x2 output. Trained on DF2K, the 7.95M-parameter model achieves a higher PSNR than every compared multi-scale method at x4 and x8 on all five standard benchmarks. At x8, it outperforms the x8-specific DRN-L on all of them, leads all compared methods on Urban100, and is within 0.13 dB of the best result elsewhere. Against three single-scale SwinIR-M models, PMS-SR uses 22% of the parameters, runs 2.9x faster on BSD100 inputs, and its outputs agree 6.7-12.4 dB more closely. Code and pretrained models will be released at https://github.com/julian135707/PMS-SR upon acceptance.

A: Infrared image super-resolution is currently led by Mamba-based networks with 26 to 37 million parameters, which are difficult to deploy on the airborne and handheld platforms where thermal imaging is most needed. This paper presents TIRMamba, a network with 896K to 910K parameters for single-channel thermal imagery. A Thermal Prior Highway computes gradient, local-contrast and spectral cues once at the input and, through one adapter per residual group, modulates a weight-tied bidirectional state-space trunk and gates its dual-scale detail branch; a tri-path reconstruction adds the learned residual to a bicubic radiometric baseline. Because the standard benchmark provides only 265 infrared training images and evaluates fusion products on full images, we train with a replay strategy: grayscale DIV2K pre-training followed by fine-tuning on 64-pixel patches drawn with equal probability from the infrared and natural corpora. At scale factor 4, TIRMamba matches the strongest protocol-trained methods on both official test sets with 29 to 40 times fewer parameters and 2.8 to 9.4 times lower latency; at scale factor 2 it gives the highest SSIM on both. A variant with prior-conditioned selectivity, TIRMamba-Rad, corrects a 3 dB raw-thermal failure of an intermediate size-invariant design and gives the best results at scale factor 4 on raw-thermal, unmanned-aerial-vehicle and independent-sensor test sets. Code and trained models will be released at https://github.com/julian135707/TIRMamba upon acceptance.

A: Fourier phase encodes important spatial image structure, but recovering an image without measured spectral magnitude requires additional constraints and leaves absolute intensity ambiguous. We propose a projection-based two-stage framework that combines Fourier-phase and spatial-support constraints with an image-specific neural prior. The first stage alternates constraint enforcement with regularized neural-prior updates, while the second performs phase/support refinement alone with guaranteed convergence. We evaluate two neural-prior implementations on the same 77 microscopy images and compare them with a constraint-only baseline. After 500 final refinement passes, the best-performing variant achieves 31.41 dB pooled PSNR, 35.75 dB mean PSNR, and 0.9531 mean SSIM, improving pooled PSNR by 1.51~dB and reducing pooled MSE by 29.3% relative to the baseline. The results demonstrate the benefit of combining neural guidance with explicit constraint refinement at the evaluated iteration budget, while showing that lower phase residual alone does not guarantee greater reconstruction accuracy.
I: In our work, we look at how Fourier phase helps capture image details. But figuring out the full picture without knowing the exact intensity is tough. So, we come up with a two-step method. It uses Fourier-phase and spatial-support rules together with a specific neural model tailored to the image. In the first step, we alternate between putting these constraints on and updating the neural model with some added smoothness. In the second step, we fine-tune the phase and support information without any more constraint work. We check out this method using 77 microscopy photos. We put it side by side with another approach that just relies on constraints. After a lot of refinement (500 times), the best model we tried out shows a 31.41 dB average in PSNR, 35.75 dB in mean PSNR, and a mean SSIM of 0.9531. This model does better than the other by 1.51 dB in PSNR and reduces the average error by 29.3%. Our study shows that mixing neural methods with clear constraints works well and that having less phase noise doesn't always mean a better reconstructed image.

A: Registering a segmented CT to fluoroscopy can locate every fracture fragment but can guide surgery only when trusted. After each shot, our closed loop registers all fragments, bounds their errors with a calibrated sandwich covariance, flags implausible or ambiguous ones, and stops or plans the next view. On simulated fluoroscopy of 60 held-out fracture CTs with realistic image uncertainty, 95% bounds covered 83% of unflagged fragments and 91% of those within 5mm, but from the second view on 14% failed by over 5mm, a third with bounds of at most 2mm. A fragment's shift when a view was added separated tightly bounded failures best (exploratory; AUC 0.94, bound 0.81). Requiring that the newest view moved no fragment beyond its bound, preferred post hoc, lowered false stops at 2mm from 23% to 6% overall, with 345 instead of 362 correct ones but more trajectories uncertified; delaying the stop did not, and other signals at equal acceptance left 10-15% false. With a segmentation error shared by all views (median Dice 0.89), 21% of this rule's stops were false against 10% without it (15 cases; exploratory). Minimax planning certified sooner than the clinical protocol without the check (4.20 versus 4.72 shots, Holm p <0.001), but no criterion reached the pre-specified endpoint, a true 2mm error, significantly sooner, even in the true basin. On real fluoroscopy of five intact pelves no 2mm certificate was false. Trust takes evidence across views, not only a calibrated local bound.

When testing this on simulated fluoroscopy of 60 held-out fracture CTs, we found that 95% of unflagged fragments were correctly covered by 83%, and 91% of fragments within 5mm were also accounted for. However, from the second view, 14% of the fragments exceeded a 5mm error. The fragment shift observed when adding a new view revealed that tighter bounds significantly improved performance (exploratory; AUC 0.94, bound 0.81). Although this tweak increased the number of correct trajectories by 345, it led to more uncertified trajectories. A: Source-free domain adaptation (SFDA) is critical for medical image segmentation as it adapts a model to an unlabeled target domain without accessing source data, thereby preserving data privacy. However, its effectiveness is often limited by confirmation bias: self-training models tend to miss small polyps, hallucinate foreground, and produce imprecise contours. We propose MedRT-SFSeg, a real-time SFDA framework built on a dual-head one-to-one/one-to-many YOLO segmentation architecture. Mask-DHF fuses precision- and recall-oriented predictions into stable pseudo-instances, while DURR uses the sign of pixel-level dual-head disagreement as a directional cue to expand or shrink masks, and additionally recovers missed instances and suppresses hallucinations. Seg-MARD further regularizes feature representations through mask-guided, region-stratified sampling. Experiments on bidirectional adaptation between Kvasir-SEG and CVC-ClinicDB show that MedRT-SFSeg achieves 80.43%/80.77% Dice and 5.53/8.44 mm ASD, improving the non-adapted baseline by 7.7 and 9.8 Dice points while running at more than 62 FPS end-to-end. These results suggest that segmentation-aware dual-head supervision can improve pseudo-label quality without sacrificing real-time inference. Project page: https://danielnguyen-05.github.io/MedRT-SFSeg

A: Sub-hourly dispatch, balancing, and storage control increasingly depend on forecasts that anticipate rapid variability in solar generation. Accurate sky-image-based irradiance forecasting requires a combination of visual cloud dynamics with recent irradiance state while adapting to different short-term irradiance-change regimes. To address this, we introduce GateFormer, a GHI-conditioned dual-decoder ViT for intra-hour global horizontal irradiance (GHI) forecasting through forecast-space decomposition. GateFormer embeds observed GHI into the visual token stream, allowing interaction with sky-image patch features through self-attention. From this shared representation, a Trajectory Head predicts future GHI sequence, while a Delta Head predicts final-horizon change from the latest observed GHI. The two final-horizon forecasts are adaptively weighted in prediction space, with magnitude- and direction-supervision targeting the remaining error. On the NREL-TSI benchmark, GateFormer attains 125.01 W/m^2 RMSE at +30 min, improving over a state-of-the-art transformer baseline by 9.6% under paired-timestamp evaluation. Across NREL-TSI, Chilbolton, and SIRTA, GateFormer achieves the lowest final-horizon RMSE among the evaluated baselines, with forecast skill of 22.97-28.86% relative to smart persistence. Component ablations show adaptive weighting outperforms both individual decoders and fixed averaging, distinguishing GateFormer from conventional forecast combination, while the supervised correction further reduces RMSE by 1.68 W/m^2 and MAE by 4.86 W/m^2. Ramp-regime diagnostics show larger gains during operationally important positive ramps, reducing RMSE by 26.27 W/m^2. These results identify forecast-space decomposition as an alternative forecasting formulation, with potential relevance to other multimodal short-horizon forecasting tasks and deployment using only sky images and measured GHI.

A: Cyclist fatality rates remain high despite policy support for active travel, and autonomous vehicles add complexity to mixed traffic. Neither crash statistics nor multi-model detection pipelines scale to continuous monitoring of perceived safety along a route. We present an edge-assisted crowdsensing system: handlebar cameras supply street-level frames, a vision-language model (VLM) turns each frame into structured traffic attributes through a single prompt, and an explainable boosting machine (EBM) combines them with OpenStreetMap road infrastructure and on-bike kinematics to predict a crowdsourced 1-9 safety score. Extraction belongs at the network edge: the fastest self-hosted model needs 2.49 s per frame and scoring takes 0.4 ms on a CPU. On 1,362 annotated frames from two London routes, the EBM regressor reaches 72.2 percent binary accuracy and a mean absolute error of 1.011 under five-fold cross-validation. It is within one accuracy point of black-box ensembles. Its per-feature shape functions give exact attribution: physical lane separation is worth +0.97 rating points, a painted lane +0.70 and a construction site -0.65. Planners can therefore price an infrastructure change in rating points, and the results enter cost-benefit analysis directly. We also report inter-annotator agreement (alpha = 0.4695), an attribute audit, and a sensitivity analysis linking attribute error to accuracy. With re-encoding, a 20 s sampling interval serves 1,000 riders at 54 Mbit/s at a cost of 1.4 accuracy points, making continuous monitoring practical.

A: Automatic extraction and anatomical numbering (R01-R12, L01-L12) of all 24 rib centerlines in thoracic CT is essential for unfolded rib visualization, fracture detection, and surgical navigation, but remains challenging due to adjacent-bone confluence, calcified costal cartilage bridges, kyphotic pose variation, and partial visibility of terminal ribs. We present ribline, an open-source three-stage framework combining: (1) an automatically detected lung-apex and vertebral-midline coordinate frame with a kyphosis-aware azimuthal angle for point ordering along each rib; (2) a hybrid voxel detector fusing an anatomically anchored Semantic Context Forest (SCF) with a lightweight 3D U-Net; and (3) a global stage that decomposes the probability skeleton into candidate curves, assigns rib indices via a bilateral Viterbi dynamic program coupled across both hemithoraces, and refines curves via template recovery and normal-plane centering (RibSnake). On the Siemens Corporate Research 2 mm thoracic CT benchmark (47 training and 12 evaluation scans), our pipeline achieves a labeled Chamfer distance of 2.05 mm, labeled clDice of 0.886 (3 mm) and 0.945 (4 mm), 97.2% labeling accuracy (278/286 ribs), and zero false-positive curves on the evaluation split, and 3.64 mm (median 2.39 mm) with 91.8% labeling accuracy across all 59 annotated scans (1,402 ribs) in 5-fold cross-validation. Code: https://github.com/wq2012/ribline Pretrained Models: https://huggingface.co/collections/wq2012/ribline

On the Siemens Corporate Research 2 mm thoracic CT benchmark (47 training and 12 evaluation scans), our pipeline achieves a labeled Chamfer distance of 2.05 mm, labeled clDice of 0.886 (3 mm) and 0.945 (4 mm), 97.2% labeling accuracy (278/286 ribs), and zero false-positive curves on the evaluation split, and 3.64 mm (median 2.39 mm) with 91.8% labeling accuracy across all 59 annotated scans (1,402 ribs) in 5-fold cross-validation. Code: https://github.com/wq2012/ribline Pretrained Models: https://huggingface.co/collections/wq2012/ribline

A: Humanoid loco-manipulation requires continuous coordination of high-dimensional whole-body motion to realize task objectives. While vision-language-action models and world action models transfer semantic and visual-dynamics priors to robot control, these priors do not necessarily capture the structure of robot motion. We introduce Kinematic Action Models (KAMs), a paradigm that treats whole-body motion as a direct pretraining target and uses a pretrained motion generator as the primary action-generation backbone. KAMs ground learned temporal and cross-body coordination priors through task conditioning, visual observations, and execution feedback. We present Kimodo-Policy as an initial instantiation, combining a frozen Kimodo text-to-motion backbone with lightweight ControlNet-based visual conditioning. A root-body-hand hierarchy coordinates locomotion and manipulation, while motion-history conditioning and repeated action-chunk prediction bridge motion synthesis and closed-loop control. Following large-scale loco-manipulation pretraining, the policy achieves the highest overall success among compared policies on multi-task HumanoidArena (72.14%), competitive performance on SIMPLE, and 60% mean success across eight real-world tasks, with 678M parameters (92M trainable). Ablations support the contribution of the pretrained motion backbone. Together, these results provide initial evidence for motion generation as a complementary foundation for humanoid action learning.
I: In our field of robotics, we're looking at how humanoid robots do locomotion and manipulation tasks. We've come up with Kinematic Action Models (KAMs) to help with this. We treat whole-body motion as something we can train directly and use a motion generator we've already trained as the main part for making actions. KAMs use learned patterns from past motion, visual stuff, and what happens when actions are actually carried out. We started with Kimodo-Policy, which mixes a set Kimodo motion model with a small-scale visual conditioning system called ControlNet. There's a main part for moving around and another for handling objects. We also look at past movements and make guesses about action chunks for better motion and control. We've pretrained this policy on a big dataset, and it works really well on HumanoidArena (72.14%), does a good job on SIMPLE, and does okay on eight real-life tasks (60%). Our policy has 678 million parameters, but only 92 million need to be trained. Ablations show the value of our motion generator. All this means motion generation could be a key step in teaching humanoids to do complex tasks.

A: Vision-language-action (VLA) models pair a vision-language backbone with an action head, but in closed-loop control the backbone sits on the control-critical path: while it computes, the robot keeps moving, so each executed action is conditioned on an increasingly stale observation. A larger backbone therefore directly blocks reactivity, especially in humanoid dexterous manipulation. We present DASH, a Decoupled Asynchronous System for Humanoids that removes this coupling. DASH splits the policy into a slow vision-language model (System 2) and a fast flow-matching action head (System 1) that run as concurrent processes over the LCM communication protocol, so the control rate is set by the action head alone, independent of backbone size. The action head fuses stale semantics from a frozen backbone with fresh vision from its own ResNet encoder, desynchronized training exposes it to the staleness it meets at deployment, and an adaptive temporal aggregator aligns overlapping action chunks under variable inference latency. On an asynchronous RoboTwin benchmark that charges inference latency in simulated time, DASH holds 20 Hz control rate from 0.8B to 8B backbones while the synchronous rate falls from 9.7 to 4.1 Hz, with higher success at every size. On a real humanoid with dexterous hands, DASH achieves clearly higher pick-and-place success than the synchronous pipeline.
I: In the field of robotics, we are looking at vision-language-action (VLA) models, which combine a vision-language system with an action head. However, we've noticed a problem. When the robot is in motion, the vision-language system can't keep up because it's busy computing. This leads to the robot acting based on outdated information, which can be especially bad for tasks requiring dexterous manipulation. That's why we've come up with DASH, which stands for Decoupled Asynchronous System for Humanoids. DASH breaks down the policy into two parts: a slow vision-language model (System 2) and a quick action head (System 1). They run at the same time using the LCM communication protocol. This lets the action head set the control speed without getting affected by how big the vision-language system is. We've trained the action head to handle outdated information and use a dynamic way to align actions with variable latency. On a RoboTwin benchmark, our setup keeps a 20 Hz control rate even for backbones between 0.8B to 8B, which is much better than the synchronous version that drops from 9.7 to 4.1 Hz. When tested on a real robot with dexterous hands, DASH definitely beats the standard approach in terms of success rates.

The issue is, while it's crunching numbers, the robot's still moving. This means the robot acts based on old data, making it hard to react fast. This is a killer for tasks like handling things in a humanoid robot's hands. Here's our game-changer, DASH. It's got this neat split between a slow vision-language model (System 2) and a quick action head (System 1). They run in parallel, chatting over the LCM protocol. Testing this out, DASH keeps up with control rates at 20 Hz for backbones between 0.8B and 8B, way better than the old 9.7 to 4.1 Hz we had with synchronous setups. Plus, on a real robot with dexterous hands, DASH did way better with pick-and-place tasks than the old-school approach. Pretty neat, huh?

A: Mobile robots operating in homes need reliable 3D perception of nearby furniture and surrounding structures, yet recovering this information on both sides of the robot's path with a single forward-mounted millimeter-wave radar remains challenging because of near-field wavefront curvature, viewpoint-dependent target visibility, and limited elevation diversity. This paper presents a motion-assisted framework for reconstructing structures on both sides of a robot's trajectory. Our near-field model relates scene reflectivity to stepped-frequency multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) observations across frequencies and robot positions using spherical paths from transmitter (Tx) to scatterer to receiver (Rx). Bilateral Tx combining provides wideband directional weighting, while sliding-aperture back-projection coherently focuses the measurements using near-field propagation distances. Top-K power fusion combines local images with different visibility. The reconstruction provides lateral-forward support for multi-layer height extraction, followed by guarded adaptive height refinement using the original MIMO channels. Experiments in controlled, office/study, and corridor environments produce mean lateral-forward localization errors of 4.65, 5.63, and 5.98 cm, respectively, with peak-to-background ratios (PBRs) exceeding 13 dB. The framework recovers bilateral 3D scattering structure from one forward pass using a single radar, without relying on learned representations of the scene.
I: In the field of robotics, specifically mobile robot navigation in homes, having a trustworthy 3D understanding of nearby furniture and surrounding structures is crucial. However, it's tricky to use a single millimeter-wave radar mounted forward to capture this info on both sides of a robot's path because of issues like wavefront curvature, visibility depending on viewpoints, and scant elevation diversity. Our work introduces a motion-assisted strategy for building up 3D structures on either side of the robot's travel route. We build a near-field model that links scene reflectivity with stepped-frequency MIMO data, which shifts with different robot positions and along spherical paths from Tx to scatterer to Rx. By using bilateral Tx combining, we get wideband directional enhancement, while sliding-aperture back-projection sharpens the measurements by using near-field distances. We merge top-K powered images, each with its own visibility, for the reconstruction. This process gives us lateral-forward aid for extracting multi-layer heights, followed by adaptive height tuning with the original MIMO data. We tested our system in controlled rooms, office/study areas, and corridors, achieving mean lateral-forward position errors of 4.65 cm, 5.63 cm, and 5.98 cm, respectively, and peak-to-background ratios (PBRs) that are more than 13 dB. This approach helps in creating a 3D scattering structure from just one forward pass of the radar without relying on any pre-learned scene details.

A: This paper presents DPGS-SLAM (Diffusion-Prior and Provenance-Aware Monocular Gaussian Splatting SLAM) for dense mapping in environments containing dynamic objects. Objects in dynamic motion remain a significant challenge for dense visual SLAM since dynamic observations can contaminate camera tracking and scene reconstruction. Although 3DGS (3D Gaussian splatting) enables efficient dense mapping, existing 3DGS-SLAM systems may exhibit instability when dynamic objects violate their underlying static-scene assumption. Excluding dynamic observations can reduce their influence on tracking and mapping, but may leave occluded static backgrounds missing or weakly constrained. Our proposed DPGS-SLAM is a monocular RGB SLAM framework that supports provisional representations of insufficiently observed static backgrounds through asynchronous diffusion-based background completion and provenance-aware Gaussian mapping. Dynamic regions are identified through optical-flow-based motion discovery and temporally consistent mask propagation by SAM2. For selected keyframes, a fine-tuned diffusion inpainting model generates plausible background appearance in occluded regions, while metric depth predicted from completed images initializes provisional Gaussian primitives. Provenance labels distinguish generated primitives from observation-supported primitives, excluding generated content from camera-pose estimation and observed-map optimization. When previously occluded backgrounds become visible, eligible generated primitives are removed, and observation-supported primitives are independently initialized from real RGB observations and predicted depth. Experimental results demonstrated competitive camera tracking, with average ATE RMSE values of 1.2 cm on TUM RGB-D and 2.7 cm on BONN RGB-D datasets. On StaDy4D, DPGS-SLAM improved average PSNR by 4.60 dB over WildGS-SLAM using only monocular RGB input.

It's all about making maps really detailed in places where stuff is moving around (you know, like in robotics). Usually, when robots try to map stuff but there's a moving object, it gets all messed up. This is a big problem 'cause these robots use cameras to figure out where everything is, and moving things can throw them off. So, we came up with this awesome way to make these robots deal with it using just one camera (that's the monocular part). Basically, we use some smart tricks to figure out what the background looks like even when it's not perfectly seen, kinda like filling in the gaps. When we're at the important moments (these are called keyframes), we use a special method to fill in the blanks in the background using something we call 'fine-tuned diffusion inpainting'. We tell the robot which guesses are made from real stuff it sees (that's the provenance) and which aren't (the guessed ones). A: Soft robots built from active materials can directly convert environmental stimuli into motion, offering a route to energy autonomy and embodied control. However, environmental energy is generally harvested at low power, whereas rapid, mechanically demanding actions require high mechanical output power. Reconciling this mismatch while sustaining self-regulated cyclic actuation is challenging, particularly at the subgram scale, where limited payload capacity constrains the integration of conventional power and control hardware. Here, we present SunLightBots, a class of subgram, sunlight-powered, untethered soft robots that achieve autonomous locomotion under continuous illumination near 1 Sun (100 mW/cm2). Their operation is enabled by a self-resetting snapping (SRS) mechanism that integrates liquid crystal elastomers (LCEs) with snap-through instability to accumulate solar energy supplied at low power, release it as rapid, high-power motion, and reset through photothermal-mechanical feedback. Through coordinated optimization of the LCE actuation temperature, photothermal conversion, actuation stress, and structural energy barrier, the system operates near 1 Sun and achieves a peak mass-specific mechanical power of 89 W/kg. At this irradiance, the optimized LCE generates an actuation stress of 0.1 MPa at approximately 60 deg C. SunLightBots demonstrate sustained swimming, crawling, and repeated impulsive jumping. Under 1.5 Suns, the swimmer advances more than three body lengths per cycle. This work provides a materials-mechanics route toward autonomous soft robots powered entirely by the environment.

It's all about liquid crystal elastomers (LCEs) that snap back when they get hot, like around 60 deg C. We crank up the SRS with the sunlight to get super-fast moves. We managed to hit 89 W/kg, which is pretty cool for these small guys. At a more intense 1.5 Suns, our sunlight-powered swimmer can move more than three times its own length in one go. It's like we're showing the world how to make soft robots that just harvest energy from light and still do some serious work. A: Navigating off-road trails on a mountain bike requires diverse locomotion skills, including aerial maneuvers, cornering, and slip recovery, paired with sophisticated perception for scene understanding. Translating these capabilities to autonomous, two-wheeled robots remains a formidable challenge. We show that autonomous, high-speed trail navigation can be achieved through a single idea: encoding the trail as a semantic layer of the terrain. In simulation, this layer embeds the navigation task into the training environment; during deployment, it is reconstructed onboard from camera and LiDAR data. First, we introduce a unified learning framework that treats local navigation and locomotion as a joint optimization problem, bypassing the twist or pose command interface of classical control hierarchies. With fixed reward weights, the same framework produces both trail racing and agile parkour, shaped only through terrain semantics and episode length. Second, our perception pipeline combines a frozen vision foundation model with a lightweight dual-head decoder that predicts per-pixel terrain semantics and confidence scores, which are fused with LiDAR range measurements into an egocentric semantic elevation map at 30 Hz onboard an NVIDIA AGX Orin. We validate our framework on the Ultra Mobility Vehicle (UMV), a bicycle robot that autonomously raced across all sections of a kilometer-long, unstructured mountain bike trail at speeds exceeding 5 m/s and averaging 3.26 m/s. In simulation, our policy fails up to an order of magnitude less often than hierarchical baselines while driving faster.

A: Micro aerial vehicles that operate without GPS often run SLAM on ARM-based edge boards, yet there is little published data on how standard RGB-D SLAM systems behave on such hardware. We benchmark RTAB-Map and ORB-SLAM3 on the Raspberry Pi 5 using six TUM RGB-D sequences at three image resolutions, recording tracking coverage, trajectory error, time per frame, memory, CPU load and temperature for every run, and we profile both systems at the stage and function level. A: Humanoid robots are expected to take over strenuous material handling in manufacturing, logistics, and healthcare, where operating existing wheeled carts would let them move heavy loads without modifying the workplace. However, humanoid cart pushing remains challenging because the bimanual grasp closes a force-coupled loop in which the contact wrenches that drive the cart also disturb the robot's balance, and payload changes alter the coupled dynamics. We propose ForPC, a force-aware whole-body control framework that regulates cart velocity through two-stage reinforcement learning. A locomotion prior is first trained under varied hand loads and upper-body postures to provide balance support. A force latent and a state latent are then inferred from onboard observations, without external force sensors, and fed to a residual policy that coordinates bounded arm, waist, and leg adjustments with base-velocity commands. Multi-objective rewards penalize bimanual internal opposition, grasp slip, and actuator saturation, encouraging the policy to apply contact force on demand without human demonstrations. Sim-to-sim experiments show that ForPC reduces cart-velocity RMSE by up to 68.2% relative to a locomotion-only baseline (Loco-only) and cross-track RMSE by up to 74.2% on the multi-bend route. Trained solely in simulation, the policy also transfers to a physical Unitree G1 without real-world training or fine-tuning and, with no payload-specific adjustment, pushes a cart carrying up to 30 kg at 0.5 m/s. These results suggest that humanoid robots could eventually replace humans for efficient material handling in daily life.

To address this, we're developing ForPC, a control framework that uses whole-body reinforcement learning. It's designed to keep the cart moving smoothly by figuring out the right balance using training with different hand loads and body positions. Then, it takes on-the-spot measurements like force and state to help with movement adjustments. We're using rewards that discourage bad balance, slipping, and overworking motors, which lets the robot push without needing human help. A: Real-time robotic perception requires accurate LiDAR semantics under limited resources. Bird's-eye-view (BEV) aggregation is efficient but can mix differently labeled surfaces in columns. We present HiPFuse, a point-BEV fusion framework that exchanges point and height-partitioned BEV features across horizontal scales, combining point-wise detail with 2D spatial context from one LiDAR scan. Fixed height assignments preserve separate vertical aggregation groups, with auxiliary supervision of initial BEV features using targets from the same 3D cells. A dual-scale BEV context module adds broader context from a coarser grid. On SemanticKITTI and MCD, HiPFuse achieves 63.7% and 62.5% mIoU at 14.2 and 22.4 FPS on Jetson AGX Orin, respectively, exceeding the 10 Hz scan rate. Separate training and evaluation show indoor applicability. Replacing only the baseline semantic front end with HiPFuse in fixed robotic systems reduces odometry absolute trajectory error RMSE by 10.6% on average across two outdoor sequences and increases accepted-loop recall by 8.7 percentage points on SemanticKITTI. Qualitative semantic maps show more continuous road labeling. Our code is available at https://github.com/haiyang2022/HiPFuse.
I: In our robotics research, we focused on the challenge of real-time LiDAR perception, specifically enhancing the accuracy of LiDAR semantics when resources are tight. We've developed HiPFuse, a framework that merges point data with BEV features across various horizontal scales. This blend leverages the detail from point data along with the spatial context of a single LiDAR scan. Our framework keeps height categorizations constant, which helps maintain distinct vertical groups. We also use extra support for initial BEV features through the same 3D cell targets. Additionally, HiPFuse introduces a dual-scale BEV context module, which gives a wider context by looking at a coarser grid. Demonstrated on datasets such as SemanticKITTI and MCD, HiPFuse outperforms baseline semantic front ends, achieving 63.7% and 62.5% mIoU at scan rates of 14.2 and 22.4 FPS on the Jetson AGX Orin. We confirmed its effectiveness in indoor settings through separate training and evaluation. With HiPFuse replacing the baseline system, we observed a 10.6% reduction in odometry absolute trajectory error RMSE and an 8.7% increase in accepted-loop recall on SemanticKITTI. Moreover, the qualitative assessment of semantic maps indicates better road labeling consistency. Our research, including the code for HiPFuse, can be found at https://github.com/haiyang2022/HiPFuse.

A: Underwater leader-follower formation control requires continuous relative-pose estimation despite degraded sensing conditions and limited onboard computation. This paper presents a reliability-adaptive multimodal perception framework for six-degree-of-freedom relative-pose tracking between two moving underwater robots. The framework integrates complementary visual, acoustic-ranging, and hydrodynamic measurements while accounting for their distinct physical characteristics and time-varying reliability. It adaptively weights modality contributions and models temporal dependencies with linear computational complexity, enabling efficient pose estimation on embedded hardware. Extensive experiments were conducted using a custom-built AUV platform, with 648 pool trials spanning two leader vehicle types, three illumination conditions, and nine trajectory patterns. Evaluation yields an average translational error of 3.8 cm and an average orientation error of 2.4°. On an onboard NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin, the fusion network achieves an inference latency of 17.62 ms, providing a 2.69-fold speedup over the evaluated Transformer-based fusion baseline. Closed-loop experiments further demonstrate stable formation maintenance with a moving leader under onboard computational constraints. A multimodal dataset containing measurements from all 648 trials will be made publicly available.

We take each type of measurement into account, 'cause they all work differently and aren't always super reliable. Our method keeps things light on resources and fast for real-time decisions on our tiny hardware, like the NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin. We tested it out on a custom-made AUV, running 648 trials. A: This work presents the 2nd-place solution (Team IF1001) to the 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge, which evaluates mobile manipulation across 100 household tasks. Our method is built on a powerful world action model (WAM), Cosmos 3. We improve Cosmos 3 by using richer visual history, task-progress conditioning, and task-group and skill-specific LoRA adapters. During inference, we apply a separate progress estimator to supply task-progress context, and use task- and progress-conditioned routing to select a task-group or skill-specific policy, complemented by action-candidate aggregation, rolling inpainting, and task-specific temporal and gripper control. To meet the minimum inference requirement of 1 FPS, we use neither recursive self-improvement (RSI) nor agentic harness methods and rely on no closed-source models; during official private-test evaluation, our system handled concurrent requests across 100 evaluation ports with limited hardware resources, sustaining an average end-to-end inference rate above 2 FPS per port. Our method achieves a mean Q-score of 0.613 and a full-task success rate of 40.9%, averaged over 3 self-evaluation rounds across all 100 tasks. A: This work presents the 2nd-place solution (Team IF1001) to the 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge, which evaluates mobile manipulation across 100 household tasks. Our method is built on a powerful world action model (WAM), Cosmos 3. We improve Cosmos 3 by using richer visual history, task-progress conditioning, and task-group and skill-specific LoRA adapters. During inference, we apply a separate progress estimator to supply task-progress context, and use task- and progress-conditioned routing to select a task-group or skill-specific policy, complemented by action-candidate aggregation, rolling inpainting, and task-specific temporal and gripper control. To meet the minimum inference requirement of 1 FPS, we use neither recursive self-improvement (RSI) nor agentic harness methods and rely on no closed-source models; during official private-test evaluation, our system handled concurrent requests across 100 evaluation ports with limited hardware resources, sustaining an average end-to-end inference rate above 2 FPS per port. Our method achieves a mean Q-score of 0.613 and a full-task success rate of 40.9%, averaged over 3 self-evaluation rounds across all 100 tasks. On the official private test set, with 20 instances per task, our system achieves a mean Q-score of 0.615 and a full-task success rate of 41.2%.

A: Many tasks compose transformations by a known rule: chained rotations in robotics and navigation. Learned models relearn it, compounding error; classical estimators hardcode it and miss hardware deviations. We impose the known structure and learn only the remainder: an exact non-commutative group law sits in the node of a self-contained layer, its edges learn local increments, and a zero-initialized correction psi learns unknown deviations of the law. A pre-training criterion predicts exact representability. On fixed-angle SU(2) composition, a 54-parameter dense edge is the most accurate dense model, at 27x fewer parameters than the strongest fixed-matrix baseline, and lies 0.05 deg above the Bayes floor. On real robot arms, an isolated 306-parameter psi reaches 1.12-1.14 mm versus 1.29-1.33 mm for Gauss-Newton at N >= 60, and the recipe transfers across three vendors and two protocols. The recipe matches classical fits where the data obey the law and loses where the imposed law is not the task's.
I: In the robotics field, many tasks involve transformations according to known rules, such as chained rotations. However, traditional learned models end up compounding errors, and classical estimators can't account for hardware variations. Here, we introduce a new approach where we use a self-contained layer that incorporates a non-commutative group law, with edges representing local increments. Additionally, we've developed a zero-initialized correction psi designed to adjust for unpredicted deviations. This method is trained with a criterion that ensures accurate representability. Specifically, we tested our model against fixed-angle SU(2) composition and found it to be incredibly efficient, utilizing only 54 parameters for a dense model, which is significantly fewer than traditional methods (27x less) while maintaining accuracy (only 0.05 deg off the Bayes floor). When applied to real robot arms, our model, with just 306 parameters, achieved a more precise result (1.12-1.14 mm) compared to the Gauss-Newton method's 1.29-1.33 mm, especially when more than 60 data points (N >= 60) are used. The success of our method is evident as it works across various settings (three different vendors and two protocols) and shows consistency, matching classical fits when applicable but acknowledges its limitations when the task deviates from the expected law.

A: Camera-based driving models build a dense bird's-eye-view (BEV) grid and spend the same computation on every cell of it, although the vehicle crosses only a few of those cells within the planning horizon. We present BEVCast, a two-stage BEV whose resolution adapts to the predicted driving path. A coarse pass encodes the whole scene on a grid of 4.096 m cells. A heat head trained on the recorded path assigns a heat to every coarse cell and the cells with the highest heat are refined into 1.024 m cells under a fixed budget. The remaining cells keep their coarse resolution, so the trajectory head reads a mixed-resolution BEV that still covers the entire scene and needs neither an HD map nor a navigation command. Against a full grid of 1.024 m cells with the same architecture and training recipe, BEVCast at a 10% refinement budget encodes 28% of the BEV queries and needs 66% of the BEV encoder time at batch size 1. On nuScenes its mean displacement error is 1.078 m against 1.149 m and its drivable area violation rate is 1.46% against 2.29%. On NAVSIM navtest its mean displacement error is 0.577 m against 0.598 m and its extended predictive driver model score is 82.51 against 81.28. Next to published planners BEVCast reaches a comparable error on both benchmarks without a navigation command. The resolution of a driving BEV can therefore follow the task instead of the grid.
I: In robotics, we're exploring camera-based driving models that create a dense BEV grid, which doesn't change regardless of the vehicle's actual path. Our innovation, BEVCast, operates in two stages. Firstly, a broad overview uses a grid of 4.096 m cells. Then, a heat map tailored to the vehicle's expected route concentrates on the most relevant cells, refining them down to 1.024 m resolution. This refined BEV still encompasses the full area without relying on HD maps or navigation instructions. BEVCast, especially with a 10% refinement budget, shows impressive efficiency—covering 28% of queries and only using 66% of the typical encoder time at a single batch size. When comparing nuScenes and NAVSIM datasets, our method demonstrates a mean displacement error reduction from 1.149 m to 1.078 m, and a decreased drivable area violation rate from 2.29% to 1.46%. Furthermore, on NAVSIM's navtest, our approach also outperforms with a mean displacement error of 0.577 m compared to 0.598 m, and improves the extended predictive driver model score from 81.28 to 82.51. Thus, BEVCast aligns closely with existing planners in performance, and dynamically adapts BEV resolution according to the driving task.

I: So, we've come up with this cool thing called BEVCast for our robotics project. Basically, it's a two-stage BEV that tweaks the grid resolution based on where the robot's gonna drive. First up, it does a coarse scan of the scene in big 4.096 m cells. Then it has this heat head that zooms in on the recorded path and gives more focus to cells with higher heat. The top 28% get this super-detailed 1.024 m resolution, while the rest stay coarse. No need for crazy high-res maps or fancy navigation commands here – our trajectory head gets the lowdown on a mixed-up resolution grid that totally covers the area. Compared to some other models with 1.024 m cells, BEVCast is pretty efficient. Even at a modest 10% refinement, it's got half the time for the BEV encoder (66% with batch size 1), but it's still pretty sharp. In terms of accuracy, on nuScenes we're talking mean displacement error at 1.078 m versus 1.149 m, and a lower drivable area violation rate at 1.46% instead of 2.29%. On NAVSIM's navtest, it beats the odds with a mean displacement error of just 0.577 m and an extended predictive driver model score of 82.51, up from 81.28. What's more, BEVCast stacks up well with published planners, nailing the results without having to deal with extra navigation commands. So, it shows that we don't need to stick to a fixed grid resolution for driving BEVs – we can make it dynamic, adapting to the task. This means we're not overdoing it with resources. Just keeping our grid resolution task-oriented is a smart move.

A: The increasing demand for real-time processing and personalized deep learning has made edge-device training essential but challenging due to high memory and computational costs. To address this, we propose a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) training accelerator with a dynamic sparse update mechanism that selectively updates important parameters using a random channel strategy, avoiding costly evaluations. Combined with activation pruning, our approach reduces activation storage to just 3.4\% of the original. Our hardware features a fused forward dataflow that concurrently processes group normalization and convolution, reducing training time by 45\% through computation reordering and efficient zero-skipping. Implemented in TSMC 28nm at FP8 precision, the design operates at 800 MHz, achieving 8 TOPS peak throughput, 31.13 TOPS/W energy efficiency, and 14.8 TOPS/mm$^2$ area efficiency, with power consumption ranging from 257 to 272 mW. The design enables on-device training within a sub-100KB on-chip SRAM budget (95KB in silicon).

We're pitching a new training accelerator for Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) that uses a dynamic way to pick out key parameters and updates them using a random channel thing. This, along with activation pruning, cuts down on activation storage to a tiny 3.4%. Our design cleverly juggles group normalization and convolution together in a fused forward dataflow, which cuts down training time by a cool 45% thanks to some smart zero-skipping and reordering. Crafted in TSMC 28nm with FP8 precision, we're talking about an 800 MHz speed with 8 TOPS peak throughput, not to mention energy efficiency at 31.13 TOPS/W and area efficiency at 14.8 TOPS/mm$^2$. Plus, it keeps power usage in check at between 257 to 272 mW. All this goodness fits in a sub-100KB of on-chip SRAM – we've actually got 95KB of that space in silicon.
